title: The Night the Universe Showed Herself
description: What happened during Navratri 2021 - and why I'm only saying it now
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
This isn’t easy for me to share or say out loud because this journey has been only mine. And while this is less than 1% of the entire journey, I feel called to share it here because Substack has given me a sense of safety.

Here goes.

Devi was never a thing in my life. Spirituality wasn’t something I bought into for the first 29 years of my life. I did practice asana, pranayama and dhyana in the name of wellness - plus it was backed by science, something my research driven, Type A, eldest daughter mind approved of.

So many things needed to fall into place for her to come to me.

Subscribe now

First, we needed a miracle I would witness - Ayurveda.

Nadi chikitsa, pulse diagnosis, followed by three nondescript bottles of kashaya - a herbal concoction that made my hair, skin, and nails glow and strengthen. I had just started with gig work and left a full time position as a Design Manager at a product company. I had the time to wait with a friend for their check up and went in for mine for moral support.

At the time my ego identified heavily with being an R1 research university graduate. I got straight to studying Ayurveda. I jumped in deep, started experimenting on my own deha - body. I learned everything I could get my hands on and started to refer to the Samhitas and Ashtanga Hridayam as if I was doing a PhD on myself.

Second, we needed a connector - the Gita.

After joining a study group for Ayurveda - my teacher was an ex-pharmacy owner from the UK, because I still needed that assurance from modern science - they offered two free Gita sessions.

The Gita started following me everywhere. Copies of it would show up at my Airbnbs, dog parks, even at home - it turns out we had a copy all along that would call out to me. My eyes would dart across the doorway to the third shelf on the bookshelf where it lay.

I was spellbound once I started my own study. I couldn’t get away from it. My research took me to Swami Sarvapriyananda and Vedanta. I felt like I was seen in these ancient tools - reading on paper, on my screen, watching video lectures - what I felt like I had known all along. A remembering more than a learning.

Third, I needed an experience of the truth in a safe space.

On the night of Kali, Navratri 2021 - about two years into this journey - my husband and I were away on vacation, deep in a forest in Andhra Pradesh. I took my fast in earnest. During a group meditation I was privileged to see the universe as it is, in its full glory.

It took a fair amount of Kriya Yoga, absolutely no expectations, and a high degree of mumukshuta for this to happen. And perhaps somewhere my vasanas and samskaras came into play.

This altered my brain chemistry for good. The universe had shown herself. I could see beyond black and white - I finally started to see not only the grey but so many colours in the spectrum. Things I had no language for before became suddenly, quietly, obvious.

At the same time, my tinkering mind had to know what I had experienced. My PhD on the self became scripture focused. I combed high and low - Shaivism, Vaishnavism, Vedanta, Sri Vidya, some quantum physics through Fritjof Capra - coupled with Samkhya, Ayurveda, Tantra. Gaining momentum slowly, leaving behind the existence I thought I understood, along with my carefully curated design career and agency.

It was especially hard because on paper I was in exactly the right place at exactly the right time.

Eventually I landed on the Devi Mahatmyam.

This study encompasses so much of everything I had explored - and rightfully so. It felt like a full circle, from one Navratri to another.

Devi had been there all along. I just needed the long way around to find her.

This piece is shared during Gupt Navratri - a personal practice, quieter and less visible than the Navratri most people know. Some things are worth saying out loud, even once.

title: The Four Purusharthas - A Summary and an Invitation
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
The ancient tradition didn’t leave the question of how to live a complete human life unanswered.

It gave us four aims. Four dimensions of a life meant to be lived simultaneously, each one sustaining the others.

Dharma - the thread that runs consistently through your life when conditioning is examined honestly enough to see it.

Artha - the energy and resources that make dharma sustainable. In today’s world that includes money, and the relationship with money that most of us inherited without choosing. Scarcity thinking, inherited fear, the unconscious ceiling that keeps artha small enough that dharma stays safely theoretical.

Kama - the desire, pleasure, and creative force that belongs in a complete human life. Not an obstacle to transcend but a dimension to inhabit honestly.

Moksha - the quality available within all three. The freedom from the patterns that keep a person living the same year in different costumes.

These four are not just a philosophy for renunciates. They are for the grahasti - the person fully inside the texture of ordinary life - who wants that life to be both genuinely inhabited and genuinely free.

How This Program Came Together

It came together the way most things worth offering do - slowly, through a combination of lived experience, honest observation, and years of paying attention to what actually moves people rather than what sounds like it should.

I spent time looking at how other mentors and coaches work. What creates genuine shift and what creates the appearance of it. What this ancient tradition offers that most modern therapeutic and coaching frameworks don’t have access to.

I looked at my own journey. The opening I had during Navratri. The years of working backwards through the texts to understand what had happened and why. The training at The Yoga Institute. The people I’ve worked with since.

What I noticed across all of it was consistent. The people who made the most genuine shifts were not the ones who learned the most, or the ones who practiced in the most strict or rigid ways. They were the ones willing to look most honestly - at the conditioning, the patterns, and at the gap between the life they were living and the one that was actually theirs.

The purusharthas became the framework not because I imposed them on the work, but because they kept revealing themselves as the most honest map available. Every person I’ve sat with was navigating some version of the same four questions:

What am I here to do? What resources do I need to do it? What do I genuinely want? And what is keeping me from being free?

The tradition named these questions two thousand years ago because they are not contemporary problems. They are the shape of a human life.

What I’ve built is a container that holds all four - not as concepts to be understood and studied, but as living questions to be inhabited. Through a combination of scriptural inquiry, reflective practice, and the kind of sustained honest conversation that most people rarely have access to.

What the Program Actually Looks Like

Ten weeks. One-to-one. Designed entirely around you.

Each session draws from wherever the inquiry requires - scriptural study, frameworks I’ve encountered from other mentors and coaches that have made a genuine difference in my own daily life, reflective practices, and whatever else the specific work calls for. These are not offered as a menu. They are woven into a coherent process rooted in understanding who you actually are beneath the conditioning - and building from there.

We look at your dharma - where it stems from, how it’s been shaped by your values and your inherited conditioning, and what it looks like when it’s finally seen clearly. We work through your relationship with artha - the money stories, the scarcity patterns, the unconscious ceilings that keep the resources smaller than the work deserves. We look honestly at what you genuinely want, and what you’ve been told you should want instead. And we work steadily toward the practical freedom that moksha points at.

The final two weeks include WhatsApp support for integration - because this is where you experience what it’s like to apply the work in daily life without the container holding you. That transition matters, and it’s part of the program.

What Becomes Possible

When the conditioning is examined honestly - when the patterns are named, the values clarified, the dharma thread made visible - something shifts in the texture of daily life.

The relationship with money changes. This is not the kind of abundance work you see with other coaches. It is not financial planning. It is looking at the stories beneath the numbers clearly enough that the stories begin to lose their authority.

The career feels different. You may or may not change your field - but the way you approach it completely shifts. You stop experiencing it as something happening to you and start experiencing it as something being built deliberately.

Relationships become more honest. Because you are no longer bringing the residue of unexamined patterns into them.

Your thinking changes. The vrittis - the mental patterns, the automatic reactions, the familiar loops that keep producing the same experience - begin to dissolve when the ground they run on has been genuinely examined. New patterns emerge. And you will start to notice, and so will the people around you, that you are lighter. More in flow. More present in an ordinary moment than you have been in years.

We will also move through scriptural references from the Gita, the Sutras, and Vedanta - as deep as the inquiry calls for - because the tradition has already mapped this territory with a precision that most modern frameworks haven’t matched.

Understanding your purpose in this human life - and approaching everything from that lens - is not an indulgence. It is the foundation on which everything else becomes aligned, sustainable, and genuinely yours.

The Invitation

Spaces are limited. Every mentorship begins with a conversation - so I can understand where you are, and you can understand what this work actually involves.

This is for someone sincere. Someone who suspects that the patterns currently running their life are not the whole of what’s possible. Someone ready to look honestly at what has been inherited, what has been chosen, and what becomes available when those two things are finally, clearly distinguished from each other.

title: Moksha - The Freedom That Was Always the Point
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What if liberation wasn’t the reward you receive after living dharma, artha, and kama correctly - but the quality running quietly beneath all three, available at any moment you are willing to look?

This is what the tradition means by moksha.

And it is also, looking back, where my own story with the purusharthas actually began.

The Night Everything Rearranged

On the seventh night of Navratri 2021 - something happened during a group meditation that I have never been able to adequately describe.

What I can say is that I saw the universe. Not as a concept. Not as a feeling of expansiveness that I later called by that name. Something more specific and more disorienting than that - a direct perception of the interconnectedness of everything, arriving without invitation, lasting long enough to reorganise something I didn’t know could be reorganised.

I came out of it changed in a way that had no immediate explanation.

What followed was not a linear spiritual awakening in the way those stories tend to be told. It was more like an instruction had been given that I spent the next several years working out the meaning of. I went back into the texts. I studied Samkhya. I deepened my relationship with Vedanta. I trained at The Yoga Institute. I built Ascend.

And at some point, working backwards through all of it, I arrived at the purusharthas - and understood, with a clarity I hadn’t had before, that what I had experienced on that seventh night wasn’t separate from the life I had been living. It was the natural culmination of a life in which dharma, artha, and kama had been - imperfectly, often unconsciously - in some kind of relationship with each other all along.

Moksha had found me before I knew to look for it.

What Moksha Actually Is

The word comes from the root muc - to release, to free, to let go. It is usually translated as liberation or enlightenment, and those translations carry enough weight to make most practitioners feel it is something very far away and very difficult to earn.

The tradition is pointing at something simultaneously more ordinary and more radical than that.

Moksha is freedom from the patterns that bind. Not freedom from life - from the recurring loops of thought, reaction, and conditioning that keep a person living the same year repeatedly in different costumes. The relationship dynamic that keeps producing the same wound. The money story that keeps creating the same ceiling. The identity that keeps requiring the same kind of confirmation. The fear that keeps making the same decisions.

This is what the yogic tradition means when it names the kleshas as the root cause of suffering - not that life is inherently painful, but that patterns of misidentification, clinging, aversion, and fear keep producing experiences that reinforce themselves. Moksha is the loosening of that grip. The moment - repeated, deepened, gradually stabilised - in which the pattern is seen clearly enough that it loses its automatic authority over the next action.

The Purusharthas Are Not a Sequence

Here is the thing I most want to say in this closing piece of the series.

The purusharthas are not four steps to be completed in order, with moksha waiting at the end as the prize for having done the other three correctly. They are four dimensions of a complete human life, meant to be lived simultaneously - each one informing and sustaining the others at every stage.

I didn’t live dharma first, then artha, then kama, then arrive at moksha on the seventh night of Navratri as a graduation ceremony. I was living all four at once, messily and imperfectly, often without knowing which one I was inhabiting. The opening on that Navratri night didn’t happen because I had completed some curriculum. It happened because the conditions were right - because enough of the conditioning had been examined, enough of the grip had loosened, enough of the artha was in place to sustain the inquiry, enough of the kama had been inhabited honestly rather than suppressed - that something could move through.

Moksha is not what happens after the purusharthas. It is what the purusharthas are in service of.

And it is available - not as a permanent state you arrive at and maintain, but as a quality of recognition that becomes more accessible the more honestly the other three are lived - at any point in the journey.

This is what made working backwards from that night so clarifying. I wasn’t looking for what I had done right. I was looking for what had been in right relationship - however imperfect - long enough for something to open.

Freedom from Patterns in Practice

Moksha as a practical orientation rather than a distant destination looks like this:

The moment you catch a familiar pattern mid-movement and make a different choice. The conversation that would usually end in the same place finding a different resolution - not because you forced it, but because something in you saw it clearly enough not to be pulled along by it. The relationship that begins to breathe because you stopped requiring it to confirm something you no longer need confirmed.

These are small. They are the texture of moksha as a living practice rather than a philosophical position.

The Bhagavad Gita describes this quality in the sthitaprajna - the one whose wisdom is steady. Not someone who has arrived somewhere unreachable. Someone who has, through sustained practice and honest inquiry, become genuinely less reactive. Who acts from clarity rather than from the momentum of unchecked conditioning. Who is present enough in any given moment to respond rather than simply repeat.

Prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān pārtha manogatān ātmanyevātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñas tadocyate (Gita II.55)

When one releases all the desires of the mind and is satisfied in the self by the self alone - that one is called steady in wisdom.

Not the absence of desire, as we explored in the kama piece. The absence of being driven by it.

That distinction - between having and being had by - is the practical edge of moksha in a human life.

What This Series Has Been Building Toward

Across these four pieces we have looked at dharma - the thread that runs consistently through a life when the conditioning is examined honestly enough to see it. Artha - the energy and resources that make dharma sustainable rather than romantic. Kama - the desire, pleasure, and creative force that belongs in a complete human life rather than being evacuated from it in the name of spiritual seriousness. And now moksha - not as the conclusion of the sequence but as the quality available within all three when they are lived with enough honesty and enough attention.

The purusharthas, taken together, are not a philosophy for renunciates. They are a framework for the grahasti - the householder, the person fully inside the texture of ordinary life - who wants that life to be both fully inhabited and genuinely free.

That, in the end, is what Ascend is here for.

The Next Step - If You Want to Go Deeper

What I’ve described across this series is a framework. What makes a framework useful is not understanding it - it is applying it to the specific, unrepeatable configuration of your own life, your own conditioning, your own particular version of each purushartha.

That application is not something that happens through reading. It happens in conversation. In the kind of sustained, honest inquiry that has enough time and enough trust to go somewhere real.

I’m opening a small number of spaces for private mentorship - a 10-week one-to-one program that moves through the purusharthas as a living inquiry rather than a conceptual study. Not therapy. Not coaching in the conventional sense. An apprenticeship in living - drawing on the Bhagavad Gita, Yoga Sutras, Vedanta, Ayurveda, and whatever else the specific inquiry requires.

This is for someone who is sincere. Who is willing to look honestly. Who suspects that the patterns currently running their life are not the whole of what’s possible - and wants to find out what becomes available when those patterns are genuinely examined.

Spaces are limited and every mentorship begins with a conversation.

If this feels like the direction - reach out. You can find more at unlockascend.com or DM me directly.

This work is an invitation to live them - not as concepts, but as the questions that actually reorganise things.

title: Kāma - The Purushartha Nobody Wants to Talk About
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What does it mean that a tradition as rigorous as the yogic one placed desire - pleasure, beauty, the full sensory experience of being alive - as one of the four aims of a human life?

This is kāma. And it may be the most honest thing the tradition ever said.

The Grouping That Distorted Everything

Before we can look at kāma clearly, we need to name something that has made it very difficult to see.

In the Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 16, Krishna groups kāma alongside krodha - anger - and lobha - greed as the three gates to darkness:

tri-vidhaṁ narakasyedaṁ dvāraṁ nāśanam ātmanaḥ

kāmaḥ krodhas tathā lobhas tasmād etat trayaṁ tyajet*

Three gates to self-destruction: desire, anger, greed. These should be abandoned.

This verse has done more to distort the conversation around kama than almost anything else in the tradition. Read in isolation - which it almost always is - it sounds like a straightforward injunction against desire. And generations of practitioners have internalised exactly that reading, treating pleasure and wanting as spiritually suspect by definition.

But the Gita is not a text that rewards isolated reading. Two chapters earlier, in Chapter 14, Krishna has already described the gunas - and established that rajas, the quality of drive and desire, is not inherently problematic. It is the unexamined, uncontrolled, ego-driven version of kama that Krishna is naming in XVI.21 - the desire that operates without dharma, without intelligence, without the capacity for release that vairagya asks for.

This is not a condemnation of kāma as a purushartha. It is a precise description of what kāma becomes when it operates without the other three aims to contain and direct it.

The grouping with krodha and lobha is a warning about kāma unmoored - not kāma in its right relationship to a full human life.

What the Kāma Sutra Actually Is

While we're correcting misconceptions - the Kāma Sutra deserves its own moment of honest reframing.

The text is almost universally understood in the West as a manual of sexual positions. It is not. It is a comprehensive treatise on the art of living well - written by Vatsyayana, a celibate scholar, likely in the third or fourth century CE. Sexual intimacy is one chapter of a text that covers aesthetics, relationship, social conduct, personal presentation, and the cultivation of a life that is genuinely pleasurable in the full sense of that word.

Vatsyayana's central argument is that kāma - pleasure, beauty, sensory experience, desire met with intelligence and refinement - is not a distraction from a meaningful life. It is an ingredient of one. A life from which beauty, intimacy, and genuine pleasure have been systematically removed is not a more spiritual life. It is a diminished one.

This is consistent with what the tradition as a whole is saying through the purusharthas. The four aims are a framework for a complete human life - not a hierarchy in which the lower three are obstacles to the fourth. Kāma belongs. The question is how it is held.

Kāma as Sensory Pleasure

I want to say something I don't hear often enough on the spiritual path.

Pleasure is not the enemy of practice. The meal that is genuinely tasted. The piece of music that moves through the body before the mind has a chance to analyse it. The beauty of a landscape that stops thought for a moment. Physical intimacy that is genuinely present rather than performed. Rest that is actually restful rather than guilty.

These are kāma in its most immediate form. And the spiritual practitioner who has systematically evacuated them from their life in the name of austerity has not transcended kāma. They have suppressed it - which is a very different movement, and one that tends to produce its own complications.

I have noticed this in myself. The seasons of practice where I was most severe about what I allowed myself to enjoy were not the seasons of deepest clarity. They were the seasons of a certain brittleness - a practice that was disciplined in form and undernourished in something harder to name.

What restored it was usually something small. A genuinely good meal. A piece of music. A walk without agenda. Not indulgence - presence. The willingness to be actually here, in this body, in this sensory experience, without immediately reaching for the next thing or translating the experience into a lesson.

That presence is kāma as a practice. And it is more difficult than it sounds.

Kāma as Creative Desire

There is a second dimension of kāma that the tradition recognises and that modern spiritual culture almost entirely overlooks.

Kāma is the force that moves things into being.

In the Rigveda - one of the oldest texts in the world - kāma appears as the primordial creative impulse. Kamas tad agre samavartatadhi - desire arose first. Before form, before structure, before the manifest world took shape, there was kāma - the wanting, the reaching toward, the force that initiates creation.

This is not the ego's desire for a particular outcome. It is something deeper - the impulse toward expression, toward making, toward the specific form that only this particular configuration of awareness can produce. It is what moves the teacher toward the student, the artist toward the work, the practitioner toward the specific shape their dharma takes in the world.

Suppressing kāma in this sense doesn't produce a more spiritual practitioner. It produces a less creative one. The work loses the particular vitality that only genuine desire - desire aligned with dharma and held lightly enough for vairagya to do its work - can sustain over time.

Kama in Right Relationship

The tradition's instruction is not to eliminate kāma but to understand its right relationship to the other three purusharthas.

Kāma in service of dharma - desire directed by the thread of one's actual purpose - is generative. The pleasure taken in work that is genuinely yours. The creative energy that moves through aligned action. The sensory richness of a life lived with full presence.

Kāma supported by artha - the resources and energy that make genuine pleasure sustainable rather than guilty or depleted. You cannot fully inhabit kāma when the nervous system is in survival mode. Pleasure requires safety. Beauty requires enough space to be noticed.

And kāma held by the possibility of moksha - which is not the elimination of desire but its eventual natural release. The practitioner who has enjoyed fully and given fully, who has inhabited the pleasures of this life with genuine presence, is often better placed to release them than the one who suppressed them for decades and still wonders what they missed.

This is the purushartha framework as an integrated whole. Not a ladder from the material to the spiritual. A web - each aim supporting and requiring the others for any of them to be fully lived.

Subscribe now

What Gets in the Way

The same conditioning we explored in the artha piece applies here - perhaps even more acutely.

The inherited belief that pleasure is suspicious. That enjoying the body is spiritually immature. That genuine rest is laziness dressed up. That the senses are obstacles to be managed rather than dimensions of experience to be inhabited with intelligence and presence.

These beliefs don't always arrive as explicit teachings. More often they arrive as atmosphere - the unspoken family understanding that comfort is not to be trusted, that wanting things is dangerous, that the appropriate relationship to pleasure is one of careful, guilty moderation.

Viveka - honest discernment - applied to kāma asks: is my relationship to pleasure actually the tradition's teaching, or is it inherited fear with Sanskrit vocabulary attached?

That's a question worth sitting with.

title: Artha - The Energy That Sustains the Path
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What if the tradition that gave us concepts like dharma and moksha also had something precise and unsentimental to say about money - and we've been too spiritually squeamish to hear it?

Artha is the second purushartha. And it may be the most misunderstood of the four.

What Artha Actually Means

The word is usually translated as wealth or money. And in popular spiritual culture, that translation tends to make people uncomfortable - as if the inclusion of material acquisition in a framework alongside dharma and moksha is an awkward concession to human weakness rather than a deliberate and intelligent design.

It isn't.

Artha comes from the root arth - meaning, purpose, resource, that which is sought. In classical usage it encompasses not just money but everything that sustains a life - energy, resources, time, relationships, infrastructure, the conditions that make it possible to live with dignity and to fulfill your dharma without being constantly depleted by the effort of surviving.

Kautilya, in the Arthashastra - one of the oldest and most sophisticated texts on statecraft ever written - treats artha with a precision that most modern economics textbooks haven't matched. He understood that a life without adequate resources is not a spiritual achievement. It is a constraint on everything else the purusharthas are pointing at.

The tradition is not saying money is the goal. It is saying that without sufficient artha, dharma becomes a luxury you cannot afford to live.

Artha and Dharma - The Relationship Between Them

Here is what the framework actually proposes: the four purusharthas are not ranked in spiritual merit with moksha at the top and artha near the bottom as a necessary evil. They are interdependent. Each one requires the others to be liveable.

Dharma without artha is noble intention without the means to act on it. The teacher who cannot sustain their teaching because they haven't built sufficient resource around it. The healer who burns out because the energy they give has no mechanism for replenishment. The practitioner who is so consumed by material scarcity that the quality of their inquiry is constantly compromised by anxiety about survival.

Krishna addresses this implicitly throughout the Gita's teaching on nishkama karma. The action is full. The energy behind it is real and sustained. What is released is the fruit - not the resource that makes continued action possible. Artha is what keeps the action going.

This is also why I think of artha not as money specifically, but as energy in circulation. Money is one form of that energy - the most legible one in the modern world. But artha also includes the physical energy in the body, the quality of attention available for the work, the relationships that sustain rather than deplete, the time that is protected rather than constantly encroached upon. All of it is artha. All of it either supports dharma or slowly starves it.

Money Energy - Where It Gets Complicated

In today's world, money is the primary vehicle through which artha moves. And this is where the conditioning we explored in the last piece - the patterns shaped by family history, survival fear, inherited scarcity becomes most visible and most obstructing.

Most people carry a relationship with money that was never consciously chosen. It was absorbed. From parents who whispered about bills behind closed doors, or who spent with a kind of desperate generosity that masked deeper anxiety, or who equated financial caution with moral virtue so thoroughly that earning well began to feel vaguely suspect.

The generation that crossed a border with nothing carried a particular kind of money conditioning - one built entirely on survival. Save everything. Trust nothing to hold. Build walls of material security high enough that what happened once can never happen again. That conditioning served a real purpose in a real crisis. Passed down two or three generations without examination, it becomes something else entirely - a relationship with money that is governed by fear rather than intelligence, and that often, paradoxically, creates the very scarcity it was trying to prevent.

The yogic tradition is unambiguous on this. What you hold in awareness, you tend to create conditions for. Yad bhavam tad bhavati - as the feeling, so the becoming. A mind saturated with scarcity thinking - regardless of the actual numbers in the account - tends to make decisions that perpetuate scarcity. It misses opportunities. It undercharges. It gives away what should be valued. It hoards what should circulate.

Money, in this sense, is not separate from the inner work. It is one of its most revealing mirrors.

Releasing the Conditioning Around Artha

The first step is simply to look honestly at the relationship.

Not the bank statement - the feeling. What arises in the body when you think about charging what your work is actually worth? What is the internal narrative around receiving money for something that feels meaningful - as if meaning and compensation are in tension rather than alignment? Where did that narrative come from, and is it actually yours?

These are not just financial questions. They are svadhyaya questions - the same honest self-inquiry the tradition asks you to bring to every other dimension of the inner life. Money is not exempt from that inquiry. In fact, given how much conditioning concentrates around it, it may be one of the most fertile places to apply viveka - the discernment that separates what is actually true from what has simply been absorbed.

Artha, tended intelligently, circulates. It doesn't accumulate behind fear-walls or drain away through unconscious patterns. It moves in proportion to the dharma it is sustaining - neither hoarded nor squandered, but held with the same quality of intelligent attention the tradition asks you to bring to everything else.

What This Looks Like in Practice

The relationship between dharma, artha, and the conditioning that obscures both is something I work with closely - and it is rarely a straightforward conversation.

What tends to surface in that work: the specific places where a person's dharma is clear but their artha is compromised - not by external circumstance but by the internal patterns that make receiving, charging, and sustaining feel more complicated than they need to be. The money stories inherited without examination. The relationship between spiritual identity and financial discomfort. The ways a person unconsciously keeps their artha small enough that their dharma stays safely theoretical.

This is the work I'm building a structured offering around - one that holds dharma and artha together as the interdependent inquiry the tradition always intended them to be.

If you're at a point where the material dimension of your path feels tangled -where you sense what you're here to do but can't quite make it sustainable -that's exactly the conversation I'd want to have with you.

Reach out. Let's look at it together.

title: Finding Dharma - Where to Actually Begin
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
If dharma isn't something you choose, like a value, but something you discern - where do you actually start looking?

Thanks for reading Ascend's Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

In the last piece, we talked about the four purusharthas. That sent me back into my own relationship with dharma as a question I'd actually had to live through.

Where I Started Looking

The first place I looked was a tool I suspect many of you have already encountered.

Ikigai.

The four-circle diagram - what you love, what you're good at, what the world needs, what you can be paid for - is everywhere. Worth knowing: this diagram wasn't created in Japan. It was made in 2014 by a blogger named Marc Winn, who merged a Spanish framework on "purpose" with a Japanese word he'd encountered in a TED talk. Ken Mogi1, the Japanese neuroscientist who has actually researched ikigai, has called the diagram a misrepresentation. Japan never produced it.

I'm naming this not to dismiss the tool but to be honest about it. I took it with a grain of salt for exactly this reason. The real concept is closer to what makes getting up worth it - not a destination found at the intersection of four circles, but a quality of attention brought to what's already in front of you.

Still - even an imperfect tool pointed me somewhere useful. As someone already on the yogic path, I had a quieter form of guidance running underneath the diagram. I was working as a design mentor at the time, and I was having a genuinely good time watching my students get placed in strong agencies and companies. That fact - the fun of it, not the achievement of it - mattered more than I initially gave it credit for.

Then I Worked Through My Core Values

This is where I went deeper, using a framework I've developed with clients that I won't fully unpack here - partly because it deserves its own space, and partly because the process matters more than the answer it produces.

What I will say is this: core values, examined honestly, don't tell you what to do. They tell you the texture of how you're meant to do anything. Mine kept circling back to teaching, mentorship, and translation - taking something dense or distant and making it usable for someone standing where I once stood.

That's not dharma yet. But it's the material dharma is built from.

What I Actually Found

Here's the part that surprised me most.

There is an overarching dharma - a theme that has stayed remarkably consistent across very different seasons of my life. Whether I was mentoring design students or now teaching the Sutras, the underlying thread hasn't moved: taking something that feels inaccessible and making it something a person can actually live by.

What changes is the expression. The specific shape dharma takes shifts with the stage of life you're in - unless a major event reroutes the direction entirely. For me, that event was the Gita finding me in 2019. Before that, the dharma was expressed through design mentorship.

This is closer to what Krishna means in the Gita, Chapter 18, Verse 47:

śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ para-dharmāt svanuṣṭhitāt

It is better to do one's own dharma imperfectly than another's perfectly - even when it changes shape entirely from what it once looked like. The constancy isn't in the role. It's in the thread underneath the role.

How to Actually Look for Yours

This is where I’ll be honest about something.

What I described above - ikigai, core values, the through-line - is the beginning of the inquiry, not the end of it. Discerning dharma isn’t a checklist you complete alone in a journal. It’s something seen more clearly with someone who can ask the question you haven’t thought to ask yourself, and who has actually walked the discernment process rather than just read about it.

I have a framework I use with clients for exactly this - tracing the thread underneath the costume, identifying what survived your life’s major reroutes intact, separating actual dharma from the roles and identities that have simply been comfortable. It’s more precise than anything I can fully lay out in a piece like this, because it’s built to respond to your specific history, not a general audience.

I’m currently building this into a structured offering. If you’re at a point where the question “what is my dharma, actually” feels less academic and more urgent - where you sense the thread but can’t yet name it - that’s exactly the conversation I’d want to have with you.

Reach out, and let’s see what we find.

What Comes Next

The next piece looks at artha - the resources that sustain the life dharma asks you to live. Not wealth in the narrow sense, but the means that make svadharma sustainable rather than romantic.

title: What My Grandfather Never Said
description: Lately I’ve been thinking about the conditioning of the human mind.
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
A film called Main Vaapas Aaunga released recently in India. I haven’t seen it yet, but the visuals in the promos are stark enough that they’ve been bringing up something else entirely - stories of my grandfather crossing the border during Partition. Stories I heard from my uncles, never from him.

He never talked about it.

How he’d brought his sisters across safely. How much fear their bodies must have stored, carried silently for decades after the actual danger had passed. How much uncertainty played on minds that had no language yet for what they were living through. One of his brothers was born in a refugee camp and has no birth certificate to this day - simply doesn’t exist on paper, in a world that runs entirely on paper. They crossed on two different trains and were separated - one half landing in Agra, the other in Indore - and found their way back to each other through something I still find remarkable: a weekly message placed in the newspaper, faithfully, week after week, until it worked two years later.

That faith has a name. Shraddha. Not blind hope - a sustained, deliberate placing of trust toward something they could not yet see the shape of.

On the surface, it’s a riches to rags to riches story. The kind that gets told at family gatherings with a certain pride. But underneath that story is something the pride doesn’t quite capture - the way that trauma doesn’t simply disappear once safety returns. It goes underground. And then it resurfaces, generations later, as a fierce, sometimes suffocating need to protect the next generation from anything resembling what was once survived.

I look at my own generation, and I see it everywhere - not always as fear, but as conditioning so deep it rarely announces itself as conditioning at all. The friend who cannot rest until every contingency has been planned for. The colleague who reads neutral feedback as an attack, because somewhere further back, criticism once arrived attached to genuine danger. The relative who measures love by how much control they’re allowed to exert, because control was once, quite literally, the difference between a family staying together and a family being separated on two different trains. None of this is irrational. It is the nervous system doing exactly what it learned to do, generations after the original danger has passed, in a body that has no way of knowing the war is over.

I’ve sat with the whats, the whys, the whens and hows of the behaviours I see in almost everyone I encounter - including myself. The impatience that isn’t really about the moment at hand. The need to be right that isn’t really about being right. The inability to sit still that isn’t really about restlessness. Trace any of it back far enough and you usually find someone, somewhere, who once needed exactly that quality to survive something the rest of us never had to survive.

This is the human experience. And it can be deeply limiting if we let it run unexamined - if we forget that beneath all this conditioning is the atman, untouched by any of it, and mistake the prison the mind has built for the whole of what we are.

But life was never meant to be only that.

We are meant to live fully - to give back through dharma, the right action that serves something beyond ourselves. To build and replenish through artha, the resources that sustain a life. To genuinely enjoy what this earth offers through kama, the pleasures that are not obstacles to the path but part of it. And, through all three, held simultaneously rather than sequentially, to move toward moksha - the transcendence that doesn’t require leaving any of this behind, only seeing it clearly enough to no longer be bound by it.

My grandfather crossed a border he never spoke of again.

I am still learning to cross the one his silence left behind.

title: Why I Went All In on the Yoga Sutras - And What Happened When I Did
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
I want to tell you something I haven’t written about directly yet.

Not a sutra. Not a framework. Just the story of how I ended up here - and why I believe the Yoga Sutras are one of the most practically transformative texts available to a modern human being living a full, complicated, ordinary life.

The Calling

A few years ago I was in the middle of building my design agency. I had just finished a deep read of the Bhagavad Gita, gone into Vedanta, studied Ayurveda. The spiritual path had been opening steadily - and for the first time in a long time, there was a particular kind of spaciousness. Not emptiness in the difficult sense. More like a clearing. Room for the next thing, without yet knowing what it was.

During the pandemic I had been sharing meditations on LinkedIn. Nothing formal - just what was present, offered to whoever needed it. The response surprised me. People came back. They asked for more. And something in that kept nudging me toward a question I kept setting aside:

Should I get certified before I do this properly?

So I started looking. And I found The Yoga Institute in Mumbai - the world’s oldest organised yoga centre, founded in 1918. Something about it resonated- the lineage not the prestige. The sense that this was a place that had held the tradition carefully and for a long time.

I knew I needed to do it.

The Decision

Here’s the part I don’t often say out loud.

At the time, every rupee/cent I was making was going back into the business. Getting certified meant going into my savings - savings I had set aside carefully, that I had built myself. I didn’t want to borrow from my then-fiancé, now husband. I didn’t want to ask family or friends.

I just knew.

Not in the way you know something intellectually. In the way the body settles when the right direction is in front of it.

I went into my savings, took out nearly $750 and into my joint account with my father and sent myself $200, less than 50% - my share. I enrolled with this $950.

What Happened Week by Week

I don’t have a clean way to describe what the four month training did to me. Quantum leap is the closest phrase - though I mean it in a specific sense. Not magic in the collectively agreed upon understanding of the word. Something I could trace back through Samkhya. Something I could recognise through Vedanta. The philosophy I had been studying started to move from the page into the body, into daily life, into ordinary moments I had been moving through on autopilot for years.

The changes were not dramatic. They were structural.

I noticed I had more control over my thoughts - not suppression, but actual space between a stimulus and my response to it. The reactivity that had defined so much of my life, the black and white thinking, the need to resolve everything immediately - it began to soften. Not because I decided it should. Because the training was reorganising something at a level I didn’t have direct access to.

The people who noticed first were not the people I would have expected. My husband noticed. My cook noticed. The people in the daily, ordinary proximity of my life - the ones who see you before you’ve had a chance to curate yourself - they noticed before I fully did.

Relationships that had carried a particular friction began to breathe. I stopped needing to assign blame, stopped seeing situations in extremes. What I had previously experienced as being villainised - I found I could meet with something close to peace. Not because I had become passive, but because the lens had changed.

I was able to look back at my own life - the choices, the pivots, the difficult seasons - and see clearly what had led to what. Without judgment. That clarity was, in a word I don’t use lightly, liberating.

A Decision I’m Grateful I Made

There was a moment in the middle of the training when I wondered whether I should learn Sanskrit properly. With my type A personality - and the discernment the training had by then given me - I could see exactly where that road led. Years of language study, done with tremendous rigour and genuine love, that would delay indefinitely the thing I actually felt called to do.

I made the decision not to.

Understanding Sanskrit deeply enough to grasp the concepts, to hold them accurately, to convey them honestly - that was what this moment asked. The full immersion could come later, and in its own time. What was needed now was to bring this out into the world.

That decision, looking back, was itself an application of the teaching. Discernment. Vairagya. Knowing when to go deep and when to move.

What the First Group Showed Me

When I began teaching - testing what I had learned with a small group - something happened I genuinely had not anticipated.

It worked. Not in a measured, outcomes-based way. In the way that you can see in someone’s eyes that something has shifted. People who came in with the same kind of fractured attention and over-busy minds that I had brought to the training started to notice the same kinds of things. The space between stimulus and response. The softening of extremes. The capacity to hold situations without immediately needing to resolve them.

I had spent years curating a design career. I was good at it. I had no idea that this - sitting with a small group and moving slowly through one of the oldest philosophical texts in the world - was going to feel like the thing I was actually here to do.

What the Yoga Sutras Are Not

Before I tell you what the study looks like, I want to be honest about what it isn’t.

It is not a certification. It will not make you a yoga teacher. It does not require prior knowledge of Sanskrit, deep experience of asana, or an existing meditation practice - though all of those are welcome.

It is also not a self-help programme. The Yoga Sutras are not a productivity system or a stress management tool. They are a rigorous, systematic, profoundly practical map of the human mind - written by someone who understood that map from the inside - and they ask genuine intellectual and personal engagement from anyone who studies them seriously.

What they give back is proportional to what is brought.

What You Can Expect

If you join the study, the first thing I’ll do is get on a one-to-one call with you sometime in the first month. I want to know where you are - what you’re carrying, what you’re curious about, what has brought you to this text at this particular moment in your life.

The sessions are live, discussion-based, and recorded - but presence matters. The energy of a small group studying together is something a recording cannot fully replicate. I ask for that commitment not as a rule but as an honest description of what makes the work possible.

What I ask of participants is simple: come willing to do real inner work. Be honest with yourself about what arises. The texts will do the rest.

Where You Might Find Yourself in One to Three Months

I’m careful about making promises. The tradition is careful about making promises. But I can tell you what I have seen, in myself and in the people I have worked with.

A different relationship with your own reactions. Not the absence of emotion - the presence of something underneath it that doesn’t move as quickly. The capacity to discern when to act and when to wait. Closer relationships that become more honest and, paradoxically, more warm - because you are no longer bringing the residue of unexamined reactivity into them.

A lens shift. That is the closest I can get to describing it. The same situations, the same relationships, the same life - seen from a vantage point that makes stuckness less sticky and clarity more available.

The victim mindset - the one that assigns the cause of difficulty entirely outside the self - begins to dissolve. Not because the difficulty disappears, but because the relationship to it changes.

This is what the Yoga Sutras do when they are studied as a living text rather than a historical one.

The August Cohort

I’m opening a small study group in August 2026.

14 weeks. Maximum 10 participants. Live. We will move through the Samadhi Pada and the Sadhana Pada - the first two chapters of the Yoga Sutras - slowly, with multiple interpretations, cross-referenced with the Bhagavad Gita, Samkhya, Vedanta, and Ayurveda where the texts illuminate each other.

Before the cohort opens, I’m holding a 90-minute workshop on June 21st - International Yoga Day - as a sample of exactly this kind of study. One sutra, explored with the depth and discussion format of the full program. INR 2000 or $31 to attend depending on where you join from. Priority access to August cohort applications included.

90 minutes of going through a deeper sutra -

We’re picking one from chapter 2. Join the conversation.

If the workshop resonates, the cohort application will feel like a natural next step. If it doesn’t, you’ll have spent 90 minutes with a text that is worth your time regardless.

title: Why the World Exists, and What You Are Here to Do With It
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
Most people come to yoga looking for relief. From stress, from the body’s complaints, from the low-grade sense that something is slightly off. And yoga, in its modern form, has become very good at offering exactly that.

What it rarely offers is what the tradition was actually pointing at.

This sutra is why Ascend exists.

The Sutra

prakāśa kriyā sthiti śīlaṁ bhūtendriyātmakaṁ bhogāpavargārthaṁ dṛśyam

Patanjali. Yoga Sutras. II.18.

The seen - the entire manifest world, everything that can be perceived, experienced, known through the senses or the mind - exists for two simultaneous purposes.

Bhoga. Experience. Engagement. The full, present, undefended inhabiting of life as it actually is.

Apavarga. Liberation. The eventual transcendence of identification with what is experienced. The recognition of what the experiencer actually is, beneath and beyond every experience.

What Most People Know - and What Gets Left Out

The conversation about yoga in the modern world is almost entirely a conversation about bhoga.

Better sleep. Less anxiety. A more present relationship with the body. Patanjali names it first and names it deliberately. The world is for experience. The body is for experience. The mind, the senses, the full texture of a human life - all of it is drishyam, the seen, and all of it exists to be met.

But the sutra doesn’t stop there. And this is where most modern yoga stops, and where the tradition continues.

Apavarga.

The word appears once in the entire corpus of the Yoga Sutras. Here, in II.18, alongside bhoga, as its inseparable counterpart. Liberation is not separate from experience - it is what experience, met honestly and completely, eventually reveals.

This is the conversation I felt called to make real - because a practice that addresses only bhoga is doing half the work the tradition actually intended. And the people I encounter who are most hungry - who have been practicing for years and still sense that something essential is just out of reach - are almost always the ones who have been given bhoga without apavarga.

They have been given the experience without the framework that makes experience intelligible as a path.

The Samkhya Foundation - What Is Actually Being Seen

To understand II.18 properly, you need the philosophical framework that sits beneath the entire Yoga Sutra text.

Samkhya.

Patanjali did not invent the cosmology he works within. He inherited it from the Samkhya tradition - one of the oldest systematic philosophies in the world - and the Yoga Sutras are, in many ways, Samkhya philosophy with a method added.

Samkhya begins with a fundamental distinction.

Purusha - pure consciousness. The witness. The aware presence that is never an object, never modified, never touched by anything that happens in experience. Purusha is nitya - eternal. Shuddha - pure. Mukta - already free. It has never been bound. It does not evolve, change, suffer, or seek. It simply is -the unchanging awareness in which everything else appears.

Prakriti - primordial nature. Everything that is not purusha. The entire manifest world - matter, energy, mind, intellect, ego, the senses, the body, thought, emotion, sensation. All of it is prakriti. All of it is drishyam - the seen.

The three qualities that constitute prakriti are the gunas:

Sattva - clarity, luminosity, the quality of knowing. Rajas - activity, movement, the quality of doing. Tamas - inertia, heaviness, the quality of being.

Everything in the manifest world - every experience, every thought, every state of practice is a particular combination of these three. Including the mind. Including the sense of being a separate self. Including the feeling of being the one who is practicing.

This is the foundation II.18 is standing on. The seen world - drishyam - is prakriti in its entirety. Bhūtendriyātmakam - composed of the elements and the senses. Prakāśa kriyā sthiti śīlam - characterised by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas respectively.

And this entire prakriti - this entire manifest world in all its texture and complexity and beauty - exists for the two purposes Patanjali names.

Bhoga and apavarga.

Bhoga - What Experience Is Actually For

Bhoga is not a concession the tradition makes to human weakness. It is not the spiritually inferior half of the sutra that serious practitioners should move beyond as quickly as possible.

Bhoga is the path.

For most practitioners - for the grahasti, the householder, the person living a full human life rather than in renunciation - bhoga is the primary vehicle through which apavarga becomes available. The relationship that breaks something open. The loss that reveals what cannot be lost. The ordinary Tuesday that, met with enough presence and honesty, shows the one who is meeting it something they could not have been told.

This is what the tradition means when it says the world exists for experience. Not that you should indulge everything - but that you should meet everything. Fully. Without the spiritual bypassing that uses practice as a reason not to be here.

The Bhagavad Gita carries this same understanding through the teaching on nishkama karma. Act fully, in the world, with complete engagement - and release the fruits. The action is bhoga - full, present, real. The releasing is the movement toward apavarga. Not two separate things happening at different times. One movement, held simultaneously.

This is why Ascend is not a renunciate tradition. The work I do with people is not about leaving the world, simplifying the life, retreating from relationship and responsibility. It is about inhabiting the life more completely - and finding, in that more complete inhabiting, the thread that leads toward apavarga.

Apavarga - What Liberation Actually Means

Apavarga comes from the root apa-vṛj - to turn away from, to separate from, to be released. It is the word the Samkhya and yoga traditions use for liberation - the release from the cycle of experience driven by misidentification.

But release from what, exactly?

Not from the world. Not from experience. Not from the body or the senses or the texture of a human life.

Release from the misidentification - the deeply rooted belief that the purusha, the witness, is the same as the prakriti through which it witnesses. That you are your thoughts. That you are your emotions. That you are the one who practices, who achieves, who suffers, who seeks. That the experiencing self is the same as the awareness in which experience appears.

This is avidya - the root klesha, the foundational ignorance - applied at the cosmological level. Purusha has not actually confused itself with prakriti. But the mind, which is prakriti, generates the appearance of a witness that is bound by what it witnesses. And liberation - apavarga - is the dissolution of that appearance.

Vedanta approaches the same recognition from a different angle. Where Samkhya maintains a distinction between purusha and prakriti even in liberation, Advaita Vedanta points at the non-dual recognition - that what you are is not a witness separate from the world, but the awareness in which both witness and world appear. Aham Brahmasmi. Tat Tvam Asi. The mahavakyas as direct pointers toward what apavarga, taken to its deepest expression, actually reveals.

These are the same territory approached from different starting points. And one of the things I find most valuable in studying the Sutras in conversation with Vedanta is precisely this - that the traditions illuminate one another in ways that neither fully illuminates alone.

Why This Sutra Is the Foundation of Ascend

When I named this work Ascend, I was looking for a word that could hold both movements simultaneously.

The engagement with life - the full, present, undefended meeting of what is here. And the movement toward something that transcends the life as currently understood. Not escape. Not renunciation. Ascent - the natural movement of awareness toward its own recognition, through the very experiences that seemed, at first, to be obstacles to it.

Bhoga and apavarga. The two purposes of the seen world. Held together, in one sutra, without hierarchy or contradiction.

This is what I felt called to make real in a teaching container. Not because the tradition is lacking teachers who can explain the Sutras - there are many. But because the conversation that holds both bhoga and apavarga simultaneously - that neither dismisses the texture of ordinary life nor stops short of what the tradition is actually pointing at - that conversation is rarer than it should be.

The person who comes to me is usually somewhere in the middle. They have been practicing. They have been studying. They are earnest and sincere and genuinely committed. And they sense, without always being able to name it, that something is missing - not in their effort, but in the framework through which the effort is being understood.

II.18 is that framework.

The world exists for your experience. And your experience, met with enough honesty and sustained enough inquiry, exists to reveal what you actually are.

Both. Simultaneously. Without needing to choose.

What This Looks Like in Practice - A Question Worth Sitting With

The study of II.18 is not complete until it becomes personal.

So here is the question the sutra actually asks - the one I would bring into a study group, the one I’d want you to sit with before moving to the next line:

Where in your life are you treating bhoga as the end point - and where are you using apavarga as a reason to avoid bhoga fully?

Both movements are available as escape routes from what the sutra is pointing at. The practitioner who only seeks experience and never inquires into the nature of the one experiencing. And the practitioner who uses liberation as a reason not to be fully here - who practices detachment before they have practiced presence.

II.18 holds both accountable. The world exists for both. And you are here for both.

That is the inquiry. And it does not resolve quickly.

An Invitation

On June 21st - International Yoga Day - I’m holding a live 90-minute workshop: Beyond Philosophy: Bringing the Yoga Sutras into Everyday Life.

This is the kind of conversation I’m describing in this piece - a single sutra, explored with depth, cross-referenced across traditions, brought into direct contact with lived experience. Discussion-based, not lecture-based. The format of the full Yoga Sutra study group, in a single session.

Attendees receive priority access to applications for the August 2026 cohort - a 14-week small-group study of the Samadhi Pada and Sadhana Pada with a maximum of 10 participants.

If this piece opened something - the workshop is the next step. I use plainer language when I teach and talk, see if it’s for you here - your body will lean in if it is.

title: Ud Jayega Hans Akela - The Soul That Flies Alone
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
I wasn’t looking for this bhajan.

I was watching Qala, a film I came to without expectations - it’s not a new movie and I didn’t think it would be anything more that an attempt to enjoy my human experience. Somewhere in the middle of it, this arrived as something that stopped the room, I paused and took it all in.

Ud jayega hans akela.

The swan will fly alone.

I’ve sat with Kabir before. The dohas, the irreverence, the refusal to be contained by any single tradition. But this particular line - in this particular moment, through this particular film - landed differently. The way things land when you are ready for them without knowing you were ready.

The teaching that finds you when the ground has been sufficiently prepared to receive it.

The Hans

In the Vedic and yogic traditions, the hans - the swan - is one of the most precise symbols available for the atman.

The swan has a quality the tradition found significant: neera-ksheera viveka - the ability to separate milk from water when the two are mixed. To take what is nourishing and leave what is not. To discern essence from appearance.

This is the atman’s nature. Not the ego, not the personality, not the accumulated identity of a lifetime - but the aware presence that moves through all of it without being constituted by any of it. The one who sees without being reduced to what is seen.

Kabir chose this image deliberately. The hans in his bhajan is not the body, not the mind, not the practitioner who has worked hard and earned liberation. It is the awareness that was always already free - and is now, at the moment the body releases, simply recognised as such.

Ud jayega hans akela.

The flying is not an achievement. It is a revelation of what was always the case.

Jag darshan ka mela

Jag darshan ka mela.

The world is a fair. A gathering. A place of spectacle and colour and noise and meeting - and then dispersal.

Kabir’s image of the mela is one of the most honest descriptions of ordinary life available in any tradition. Not a condemnation of the world - Kabir was no ascetic. He was a weaver. A householder. A man who lived fully inside the texture of ordinary life and saw it clearly from within.

The mela is not wrong. It is not something to escape. It is what it is - a temporary gathering, a moment of meeting, a fair that is already in the process of ending even as it reaches its height.

What the bhajan is pointing at is not the wrongness of the mela, but the confusion that arises when the hans - the atman - forgets that it is a visitor to the fair rather than constituted by it. When the temporary gathering begins to feel like the permanent home. When the noise of the mela becomes the only reality, and the quiet that preceded it and will follow it becomes unimaginable.

Jag darshan ka mela zaag ke.

The world’s fair - wake up from it. Jaagna - awakening. The eyes opening while still inside the fair. The recognition, without leaving the gathering, that what you are is not what the gathering contains.

This is the grahasti’s path carried to its deepest implication. You do not need to leave the mela. You need to see it clearly while you are inside it.

The Aloneness

Ud jayega hans akela.

The line that stopped the room for me.

The aloneness Kabir is pointing at - akela - is not loneliness. It is not the isolation of someone who has been left behind or who has withdrawn from life. It is something more fundamental and, once recognised, more liberating than anything the opposite of loneliness can offer.

The atman makes its journey alone. Kabir understood relationship as deeply as anyone in the tradition. But because the nature of the atman is such that it cannot be accompanied in the way the ego imagines accompaniment. No one else’s understanding substitutes for your own recognition. No teacher’s realisation transfers directly into the student’s awareness. No relationship, however profound, can make the journey that each awareness must make for itself.

If the journey is ultimately alone, then the preparations for it - the practice, the inquiry, the honest self-study - are not about performing for an audience or accumulating approval. They are between you and what you actually are. The aloneness of the hans is the most radical possible freedom from the need for external validation of the inner life.

Subscribe now

The Serendipity

There is a particular quality of encounter with a teaching that arrives sideways - through a film, through a song heard in passing, through a conversation that was supposed to be about something else entirely.

The tradition has a word for the readiness that makes such encounters possible. Patra — the vessel. The one who has been prepared to receive, without knowing the preparation was happening.

I don’t know exactly when I became patra for this bhajan. Possibly it was always waiting — for the particular combination of what had been understood and what had not yet been released that made the line land the way it did in that room.

What I know is that Kabir did not write for scholars. He wrote for the person sitting in the middle of their ordinary life, suddenly stopped by something that arrived without announcement and rearranged something they didn’t know needed rearranging.

Ud jayega hans akela.

If it has arrived for you now in this piece, through this reading that is not coincidence.

The mela is still playing. The hans already knows the way.

There is more that I found….

There is more I found in this deep dive - anecdotes about Kabir that I've held back from the main piece. Not because they aren't fascinating, but because they touch on religious history in a way that isn't what Ascend is here for. This work is rooted in Sanatana Dharma - the eternal inquiry - not in any religion's claim over it. Kabir himself would probably approve of that boundary. title: Abhinivesha - The Fear That Runs Deepest
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What is the one obstruction that runs even in the wise? The one klesha that doesn’t require ignorance or conditioning to sustain itself - but persists, Patanjali says, in every embodied being?

Abhinivesha.

What Is Abhinivesha in Yoga?

Patanjali defines it in Sutra II.9:

svarasavāhī viduṣo ‘pi tathā rūḍho ‘bhiniveśaḥ

Abhinivesha flows by its own momentum - svarasavahi - and is deeply rooted - rudha - even in the learned. Even in the wise. Even in those who know better.

This is what makes abhinivesha the most humbling of the five kleshas. Avidya can be addressed through knowledge. Asmita can be loosened through honest self-study. Raga and dvesha can be worked with through sustained practice and viveka. But abhinivesha - the deepest clinging, the fear that runs beneath all other fears - persists by its own momentum regardless of how much you know.

It is the fifth and final klesha in Sutra II.3

avidyā asmitā rāga dveṣa abhiniveśāḥ

And it is, in the tradition’s understanding, the one that sits closest to the root of embodied existence itself.

The Three Faces of Abhinivesha

Abhinivesha is most commonly translated as the fear of death. And it includes that - the instinctive, biological clinging or survival instinct to physical existence that runs in every living system regardless of philosophical understanding. You can know, intellectually, that the atman is deathless. And the body will still flinch from the edge.

But abhinivesha operates at three levels simultaneously - and on the spiritual path, it is the second and third that become most relevant.

The fear of death - the literal level. The clinging to physical continuity, to the body, to the life as it is currently configured. This is svarasavahi - self-sustaining, instinctive, not requiring thought to perpetuate itself. It runs in the cells before the mind has a chance to intervene.

The fear of transformation - the psychological level. The resistance to becoming what practice is genuinely asking you to become. Not the dramatic resistance - the subtle one. The practitioner who keeps their practice safe enough that it never asks too much. Who studies the texts but stops just short of the inquiry that would require something to change. Who understands the teaching intellectually but finds, again and again, a reason not to let it reorganise their life.

This is abhinivesha operating through the personality rather than the body. The fear is not of physical death but of the death of a way of being - a role, a relationship, a self-concept - that practice is quietly asking to be released.

The fear of dissolution - the deepest level. The terror that arises, in genuinely advanced practice, at the prospect of the self dissolving entirely. The resistance to para vairagya. The point at which the practitioner who has spent years releasing the grip suddenly finds that the final releasing - of the one who has been doing all the releasing - is the most frightening thing practice has ever asked.

This is what Patanjali means by rudha - deeply rooted. Rooted not in conditioning or ignorance, but in the fundamental structure of individual existence itself. The sense of being a separate self does not want to dissolve, even when it understands that dissolution is liberation.

These three are not necessarily sequential - They are the same movement at different depths of the system - the body flinching from physical death, the personality resisting transformation, the self contracting from dissolution. Abhinivesha all the way down.

Why It Runs Even in the Wise

This is the line in Sutra II.9 that deserves the most honest attention.

Viduṣo ‘pi - even in the learned. Even in those who know.

Most obstructions can be addressed through knowledge. Avidya - ignorance - dissolves through correct understanding. Asmita loosens when the mahavakyas are held as genuine inquiry rather than intellectual position. But abhinivesha persists by its own momentum - svarasavahi - independent of how much the practitioner knows about its nature.

This is a description of the terrain that honest practice eventually enters - where knowledge is no longer sufficient, where understanding no longer leads directly to freedom, where something more than intellectual comprehension is required.

What is required is what the tradition has always pointed toward beneath the philosophy. Direct experience of what the philosophy is describing. Not the concept of the deathless atman - the recognition of it, in the body, as one’s own nature.

This is also why abhinivesha cannot be worked with through more of the same practice that addressed the earlier kleshas. It requires a qualitative shift - from practice as something the practitioner does, to practice as something that does the practitioner.

Krishna on Abhinivesha - The Deathless Atman

The Bhagavad Gita opens, in many ways, as a direct response to abhinivesha.

Arjuna on the battlefield is not simply afraid of violence. He is confronting, at the deepest level, the fear of loss - of his teachers, his family, his role, his identity as a warrior, his sense of what his life has meant. This is abhinivesha in its psychological and existential dimensions - the clinging to what is known, to what has been, to the continuity of a self whose dissolution feels intolerable.

Krishna’s response begins in Chapter 2 with the most direct possible antidote:

na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ ajo nityaḥ śāśvato ‘yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre (II.20)

The atman is never born and never dies. It has not come into being and will not come into being. It is unborn, eternal, ever-existing, primeval. It is not slain when the body is slain.

This is not consolation philosophy. Krishna is pointing at the direct antidote to abhinivesha - not the suppression of fear, but the recognition that what you fundamentally are has never been subject to the threat that fear is responding to.

The body dies. The role ends. The self-concept dissolves. The personality transforms beyond recognition. And the atman - ajo nityaḥ śāśvatah - unborn, eternal, unchanging - remains. Not as a future state. As the present reality that abhinivesha obscures.

This is also where the Gita’s teaching on karma yoga finds its deepest relevance. When the practitioner is no longer identified with the outcome - when nishkama karma is not just a philosophical commitment but a lived orientation - abhinivesha loses the ground it needs to sustain itself. The fear of death requires a self that can die. The fear of transformation requires an identity that can be threatened. When vairagya has sufficiently loosened the grip on both, what remains is the awareness that was never in danger.

Abhinivesha on the Spiritual Path

For practitioners who have been on the path for some time, abhinivesha tends to show up in specific and recognisable ways.

The study that goes right to the edge of a genuine insight - and then turns back toward the familiar. The practice that has become sophisticated enough to be comfortable - and therefore safe enough to never quite ask everything. The teacher or teaching that is kept at a slight intellectual distance, appreciated but not allowed to fully land. The transformation that is understood, endorsed, spoken about with genuine enthusiasm - and quietly not inhabited.

In each case the structure is the same. Something in the system has recognised that what is being asked - by the text, the practice, the teacher, the moment - would require a genuine dissolution of something it has been sustaining. And it has found, without conscious decision, a way to stop just short.

This is abhinivesha operating as the spiritual path’s most subtle guardian. Not preventing practice - directing it. Keeping it productive enough to sustain the practitioner’s identity as someone who practices, but safe enough that the practitioner remains intact.

Viveka - sustained discernment - is what makes this visible. And what makes it visible is what begins, slowly, to loosen it.

The Antidote - Shraddha and Vairagya

Abhinivesha cannot be dissolved through effort. The one who is afraid cannot think their way out of the fear, practice their way past it, or accumulate enough knowledge to render it irrelevant. Patanjali is clear - it runs by its own momentum even in the wise.

What moves through abhinivesha is a different quality entirely.

Shraddha - the trust that what lies beyond the dissolution is not annihilation but recognition. The faith - held in the heart, not merely the intellect - that the atman Krishna describes in II.20 is not a concept but a reality. That the open hand will be held by something the closed fist could never receive.

Shraddha does not eliminate the fear. It creates enough safety in the system that the fear can be present without the system immediately contracting around it. The body still flinches. The personality still resists. But underneath both, something knows - svarasavahi in the opposite direction - that the dissolution being feared is not what it appears.

Vairagya - the freedom of the open hand - is what shraddha makes possible. When trust is sufficiently established, the releasing that abhinivesha has been preventing becomes available. Not as a dramatic moment of surrender, but as a gradual easing - the grip loosening fraction by fraction across the length of a sustained and honest practice.

Together, shraddha and vairagya are the two sadhaka tattvas that most directly meet abhinivesha. Faith creates the safety. Non-attachment creates the freedom. And between them, what practice is asking for finally becomes possible - not because the fear has been eliminated, but because it is no longer the last word.

What Abhinivesha Ultimately Points At

There is something worth sitting with in the fact that Patanjali names abhinivesha as the fifth and final klesha - the one that persists even after the others have been significantly addressed.

It is not a design flaw in the system. It is the tradition’s honest acknowledgment that the path, taken seriously, eventually arrives at a threshold that knowledge and effort alone cannot cross.

At that threshold, the practitioner meets something that all the earlier practice has been preparing them for - the direct recognition that what they are was never the thing that abhinivesha was trying to protect.

Na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre. Not slain when the body is slain.

Not as a belief. Not as a consolation. As the most immediate, pratyaksha, directly perceptible truth available - when the layers that have been obscuring it have been sufficiently thinned by everything this series has been exploring.

The fear runs deep. The awareness in which it runs is deeper still.

And it was never in danger.
