title: meditations of a millennial grahasti : note 01
description: Notes from inside an ordinary argument
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
Musings of a sadhak still working on their abhyas.

Preface

This is the experience of a situation that came up as a partner, as a pet parent, as a karma yogi, as a designer, as a human. I felt called to share this note I penned down after a normal everyday ‘argument’, You might notice an inconsistency in sentence structure and grammar - I’ve copied my note as is.

I use the word 'awakening' here loosely - not as a claim of arrival, but as shorthand for a shift in the quality of observation. What I mean more precisely is a state of reduced identification with the vrittis. The tradition would call it closer to sakshibhava, the witness stance - than any final ‘realisation’.

The following in a keen observation of the vrittis that came up in the seconds that followed the interaction - unedited, mid-breath, in the minutes after.

The Note

Context

Most days are calm and composed, filled with intense sadhana and reflection. Then, inevitably in surrender, or after irregular sadhana something comes up. At this point you know drg and drshya, so your experience is amazing - you may be grieving outwardly but since it’s easier to break through your ego, you can discern the real from unreal.

You start to look for the lessons in this situation.

You also understand your ego well, your conditioning, you see the human problems at the scale that you used to (before awakening). You give in for a moment to feel the human emotions. You’re seeing your ego solve it(the perceived problem) with a human lens.

Vritti sarupyam itaratra

(Patanjali’s Sutra 1.4)

The seer identifies with the fluctuations of the mind

You’re not rigid enough to judge what’s happening. You’re the observer.

You can see yourself (the ego) try to maneuver through this. You see your mind try to solve this with the depth of knowledge you have on nervous system regulation (intellectualizing.

Watching your old patterns for a flicker till your cognizance kicks in.

What a ride.

How beautiful!

‘I’m privileged’ says you(r soul), as you observe swirling vrittis of ayurvedic knowledge (and experience) the familiar bodily queues1 from years of ayurvedic svadhyay intermingle with vrittis of Vedic, Puranic, Upanishadic knowledge on modern physiology and psychology.

Tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam

(Patanjali’s Sutra 1.3)

Then the perceiver is situated in his own form.

You don’t try to do anything. Just observe without judgement & without labelling as the vrittis dissolve.

‘What a ride indeed’ you hear yourself proclaim as you reach out for your pen and journal now back to regulated breath.

title: Vairagya - The Freedom of the Open Hand
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What if non-attachment wasn’t about caring less - but about being free enough to care completely, without the caring becoming a cage?

This is the most liberating reframe the yogic tradition offers.

And it lives at the heart of vairagya.

What Is Vairagya in Yoga?

Vairagya is usually translated as non-attachment, dispassion, or renunciation. All three translations are incomplete in the same way - they suggest a pulling away, a withdrawal, a cooling of engagement with life.

The word itself broken down looks like this-

Vi - without, free from.

+

Raga - the clinging, the colouring, the grip that pleasure leaves behind.

Vairagya is not the absence of feeling. It is freedom from the compulsion that feeling generates when it hardens into demand.

Patanjali places vairagya alongside abhyasa in Sutra I.15 as one of the two foundations of practice:

dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayavitṛṣṇasya vaśīkārasaṁjñā vairāgyam

Vairagya is the mastery - vasikara - that arises when thirst for both seen and heard objects has been released. Not suppressed. Released. The distinction matters enormously.

And in Sutra I.16 he names its highest expression:

tat paraṁ puruṣakhyāter guṇavaitṛṣṇyam

Para vairagya - supreme non-attachment - is the freedom from thirst even for the gunas themselves. Not just freedom from objects of experience, but freedom from the fundamental qualities of nature - rajas, tamas, sattva - that generate all experience.

This is the full spectrum. Apara vairagya - the preliminary - begins with releasing the grip on specific objects, experiences, and outcomes. Para vairagya is what that releasing, sustained over time through viveka and honest practice, eventually becomes - a freedom so complete that even the most refined spiritual experiences are held lightly.

Vairagya ≠ Indifference

This is the misreading worth dismantling before anything else.

Genuine vairagya is warmer than attachment, not cooler. Because when the grip is released - when you are no longer requiring the experience to repeat itself, the person to return your love in the exact form you offered it, the practice to feel the way it once felt - what remains is presence. Full, undefended, ungrasping presence.

You feel more, not less. You love more completely, not more carefully. You engage with life more directly, not from behind the glass of managed expectation.

This is the paradox at the heart of vairagya. The open hand receives more than the closed fist ever could.

The Sthitaprajna | Krishna’s Portrait of Vairagya

In Chapter 2 of the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna a direct question:

sthitaprajñasya kā bhāṣā samādhisthasya keśava

What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady? How does one established in samadhi speak, sit, move?

Krishna’s answer across verses 2.55-2.72 is the most complete portrait of vairagya in lived experience available in the tradition.

prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān pārtha manogatān ātmany evātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñas tadocyate (II.55)

When a person completely releases all desires of the mind and is satisfied in the self by the self alone - that one is called sthitaprajna. Steady in wisdom.

The sthitaprajna is not someone who has stopped desiring because life has given them everything. They are someone in whom the source of satisfaction has been correctly located - not in objects, experiences, or outcomes, but in awareness itself.

Krishna continues. The sthitaprajna is not moved from their centre by sorrow. They do not reach for pleasure. Free from attachment, fear, and anger. Like a lamp in a windless place - acalā - that does not flicker (II.67).

This is apara vairagya becoming para vairagya through sustained practice (This is not easy). The preliminary releasing of specific objects gradually deepens into a fundamental reorientation - the self no longer seeking completion through experience because it has recognised itself as already complete.

Vairagya Across This Series

Looking back across the badhaka and sadhaka tattvas - the obstructing and supporting principles we have moved through together - vairagya was present in every piece as the quality that each one was building toward.

Rigidity is the absence of vairagya in practice - the clinging to a fixed form because releasing it feels like losing something essential. Prayas is the absence of vairagya in effort - the inability to stop because stopping feels like failure. Asmita is the absence of vairagya in identity - the clinging to the practitioner self because the self without its practice feels insufficient. Raga is the absence of vairagya in experience - the reaching toward the repetition of what was once real.

And on the sadhaka side - viveka produces vairagya. Santosha expresses vairagya. Tapas burns away what vairagya releases. Ishvarapranidhana is vairagya directed toward the source itself.

The entire series has been, in some sense, a map of what vairagya looks like when it is absent - and what practice looks like when it is gradually, patiently restored.

Apara to Para - The Spectrum of Practice

Vairagya does not arrive fully formed. It develops - beginning as a deliberate practice and deepening, over time, into something more natural than the clinging it replaced.

Apara vairagya begins in the ordinary. The meal that is eaten without immediately planning the next one. The session that is allowed to be unremarkable without that unremarkableness meaning something about you. The relationship that is loved fully without the loving becoming a demand for a particular response.

These are not small things, they are the daily practice of releasing the grip before it hardens. Each releasing is apara vairagya in action - small, consistent, cumulative.

Over time, something shifts. The releasing becomes less effortful. The grip doesn’t form as quickly. The residue that pleasure leaves - what Patanjali names in II.7 as raga - begins to thin.

Para vairagya is not a destination you arrive at through sufficient apara practice. It is more accurate to say that para vairagya is what apara vairagya reveals has always been present. The freedom that was always the nature of awareness - before raga, before the kleshas, before avidya constructed the sense of a separate self that needed experience to be complete.

This is vivekajam jnanam - the knowledge born of discernment - applied to the practitioner’s own nature. Seeing clearly that what you are was never bound by what you experienced. That the open hand was always the original position. That the grip was learned, not innate.

Vairagya and Shraddha - The Balance the Path Requires

There is a tension worth naming.

Vairagya without shraddha - without the faith and trust we explored in the ishvarapranidhana piece - can become a kind of spiritual dryness. The practitioner who has released attachment to outcomes but has not cultivated the quality of trust that makes release feel like freedom rather than emptiness.

This is where the two work together. Shraddha is what makes vairagya warm rather than cold. The releasing is not into a void - it is into the intelligence that was always operating beneath the grip. The open hand is not empty. It is held by something larger than what it was holding.

Krishna names this directly. The sthitaprajna is atmanyevatmana tushtah - satisfied in the self by the self alone. Not satisfied through emptiness, but through the recognition of the self as already full. Vairagya is what removes the obstruction to that recognition. Shraddha is what allows the recognition to be trusted when it arrives.

A Practical Framework for Cultivating Vairagya

Begin with noticing the grip. Not releasing it - noticing it. Where in your practice, your relationships, your daily life is the hand closed? What is it holding? What does it believe it will lose if it opens? Svadhyaya applied to raga is the beginning of vairagya.

Practice completing experiences. Vairagya develops when experiences are allowed to be whole in themselves rather than immediately reaching for their continuation. The session ends - let it end. The meal is finished - let it be finished. The conversation completes - let it complete. Each small completion is the open hand practicing its natural position.

Return to the source rather than the object. The clarity, the openness, the sense of recognition that arose in that experience - trace it back to awareness itself rather than to the occasion that produced it. This is viveka supporting vairagya directly. When the source is correctly located, the grip on the object begins to loosen on its own.

Hold the sthitaprajna as a living question. Not as an ideal to achieve - as a mirror. In this moment, in this situation, what would the one established in vairagya do? The question, returned to consistently, begins to reorganise the relationship to experience from the inside.

Allow vairagya to be gradual. The tradition is clear - para vairagya is not produced by effort. It is revealed through sustained, patient practice that gradually removes what obscures it. The practitioner who tries to force non-attachment is practicing the opposite of vairagya. The one who shows up consistently, releases what they can, and trusts the process - that practitioner is already in the movement.

What Vairagya Actually Feels Like

It rarely announces itself as liberation.

It feels like noticing, one ordinary day, that something which used to pull at you simply doesn’t pull as strongly. That the session which felt inadequate last year would feel like enough today. That the outcome you once needed has become something you genuinely prefer but no longer require.

It feels like the grip easing - incrementally, almost imperceptibly, across the length of a sustained practice.

And then, occasionally, in a moment that cannot be predicted or produced - the open hand. The complete absence of the reaching. The recognition that what you are has never been diminished by what you didn’t receive, never been completed by what you did.

Atmanyevatmana tushtah. Satisfied in the self by the self alone. As a lived, ordinary, unremarkable moment of genuine freedom.

title: Raga - The Clinging That Feels Like Love
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What if the problem was never feeling too much but clinging to what was felt? What if the tradition never asked you to become cold, detached, or untouched by life only free from the grip that turns experience into bondage?

This is the most misunderstood dimension of the yogic path.

And raga is at the centre of it.

What Is Raga in Yoga?

Patanjali defines raga in Sutra II.7:

sukha-anuśayī rāgaḥ

Raga is what follows pleasure. The residue that pleasure leaves - the wanting of it again, the reaching toward its repetition, the contraction that happens when it doesn’t return.

It is the third klesha in Patanjali’s sequence

avidyā asmitā rāga dveṣa abhiniveśāḥ

- II.3

It arises from asmita, the identified self because a self that believes it is separate will always seek completion through experience. Raga is that seeking given a specific object.

The session that once opened something real. The teacher whose words landed like recognition. The state of practice that felt like home. The version of yourself that existed before the path asked something difficult of you.

None of these objects are wrong. The clinging to them is what becomes the obstruction.

What the Tradition Says About Feeling

This is where the yogic path gets misread, sometimes deliberately, sometimes through the flattening that happens when depth gets simplified for wide distribution.

The tradition does not ask for detachment in the sense of coldness. It does not ask you to stop feeling, stop loving, stop being moved by what is beautiful or true or devastating. A practice that produces emotional flatness has not dissolved raga - it has suppressed it, which is a different movement entirely and one that tends to resurface with considerable force.

What the tradition asks for is something more precise and more difficult.

Unattachment. The absence of the grip that turns feeling into demand.

You feel fully. You love completely. You are moved by what deserves to move you. And you do not require the feeling to stay, the love to be returned in the exact form you offered it, or the experience to repeat itself in order to validate what it was when it was present.

This is the distinction, raga asks you to sit with to see whether the feeling owns you.

Subscribe now

How Raga Operates in Practice

Raga in practice is subtler than it first appears.

It is the practitioner who returns again and again to the same sequence because it once produced something extraordinary no longer asking whether it is what this moment needs, but demanding that the moment reproduce what a previous moment gave.

It is the student who cannot hear a teaching from anyone other than the teacher who first opened something in them even when that teacher has nothing more to offer, or when a different voice is carrying exactly what is needed now.

It is the relationship to a particular state of practice - the clarity, the stillness, the sense of expansiveness that becomes the measuring instrument of every session. When the state is present, practice feels alive. When it isn’t, something has gone wrong. The state itself has become the object of raga.

And it is the clinging to a previous version of the self - the one who practiced before life got complicated, before the path asked something difficult, before the identity that practice had built began to be dismantled by the very practice that built it.

In every case, the structure is the same. Something real was experienced. The experience left a residue. The residue became a demand. And the demand is now generating suffering not because the original experience was wrong, but because the clinging to its repetition has closed off what the present moment is actually offering.

The Gita on Raga - Sangha and Its Consequences

The Bhagavad Gita approaches raga through the language of sangha - attachment and traces its consequences with unusual precision.

In Chapter 2, verses 62-63, Krishna describes the chain:

dhyāyato viṣayān puṁsaḥ saṅgas teṣūpajāyate saṅgāt sañjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodho ‘bhijāyate

Contemplating sense objects, attachment arises. From attachment, desire. From desire, anger. From anger, delusion. From delusion, loss of memory. From loss of memory, loss of discrimination. From loss of discrimination - naśyati - destruction.

Raga begins with something entirely innocent - noticing what brings pleasure, what opens something, what feels like recognition. The problem is not the noticing. It is what happens next when the noticing becomes dwelling, and the dwelling becomes demand, and the demand is not met.

Krishna’s prescription is not to stop noticing. It is to act, engage, feel and release. The full presence of bhoga without the grip of raga. This is nishkama karma applied to the inner life - not the suppression of pleasure, but the freedom from being controlled by its memory.

Raga and Avidya - The Root Connection

Like every klesha, raga is ultimately an expression of avidya - the root ignorance.

The clinging that raga generates is always, at its base, the clinging of a self that believes it is incomplete. That the peak experience, the right teacher, the perfect state of practice, the earlier version of itself contains something it needs in order to be whole.

Viveka, sustained discernment, sees through this. Not by suppressing the feeling that arises when something real is experienced, but by recognising that what was felt in that moment was not produced by the object. The clarity, the openness, the sense of recognition - these arose from awareness itself. The object was a pointer. Raga mistakes the pointer for the source.

This is the practical intelligence behind the tradition’s insistence on non-attachment. Not because the world is not worth experiencing - Sutra II.18 makes clear that it is. But because the source of what is most real in every experience is not outside. And raga, sustained, is the ongoing insistence that it is.

Working With Raga - Toward Unattachment

The movement through raga is not a practice of suppression or forced letting go. It is a gradual reorientation- the same quality of patient heat that tapas provides, applied to the specific objects of clinging.

Notice the residue. After an experience that produces pleasure like a good session, a meaningful exchange, a moment of genuine clarity notice what remains. Is there gratitude for what was present? Or is there immediately a reaching toward its repetition? That noticing, done honestly, is svadhyaya applied to raga directly.

Return to the source rather than the object. The clarity you experienced in that session - where did it actually come from? The teacher whose words opened something - what was already present in you that made those words land? Tracing the experience back to awareness itself, rather than to its occasion, begins to loosen raga’s grip without requiring the experience to be devalued.

Allow bhoga to be complete in itself. Each experience, fully met, is already whole. The meal doesn’t need to be remembered to have nourished. The session doesn’t need to be repeated to have opened something. When experience is allowed to be complete - received fully and released fully - raga has nothing to hold.

Practice in the ordinary. Raga feeds on the extraordinary. The peak session, the inspired day, the teacher who seems to have all the answers. A practice that can only be sustained when conditions are exceptional is a practice quietly governed by raga. Returning to the ordinary - the unremarkable Tuesday, the session where nothing dramatic happens - is the most direct available antidote.

Where raga is the grip, vairagya is the open hand.

title: Agni - Why Your Digestive Fire Is the Root of Everything
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
Why do two people eat the same meal and feel completely different afterward? Why does stress show up on your skin before it shows up anywhere else? Why does summer, of all seasons, leave some people feeling sluggish and inflamed?

In Ayurveda, the answer to all three is the same. - Agni.

Thanks for reading Ascend's Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

What Is Agni in Ayurveda?

Agni is the Sanskrit word for fire. In the Ayurvedic framework, it refers to the metabolic intelligence that governs digestion - not just of food, but of everything the system takes in. Sensory experience. Emotion. Information. Stress.

Every cell in the body has its own agni. But the seat of the whole system is jatharagni - the digestive fire that lives in the gut. When jatharagni is strong and balanced, the body transforms what it receives into nourishment. When it is weak, irregular, or overwhelmed, what should become nourishment becomes something else - heaviness, inflammation, unprocessed residue that Ayurveda calls ama.

Ama is literally undigested matter. And it is, in the Ayurvedic view, the root of most disease.

This is why agni is not just a digestive concept. It is a foundational one.

Agni in Summer - Why the Heat Doesn't Help

This might seem counterintuitive. Summer is hot. Agni is fire. Surely more heat means stronger digestion?

Not quite.

In Ayurveda, summer is governed by pitta dosha - the principle of fire and water. When the external environment heats up, the body's internal fire is already working harder to manage that heat. The digestive system, in a kind of protective intelligence, actually moderates itself in summer. Jatharagni becomes more sensitive, more reactive, and less tolerant of the foods and habits that it might handle easily in cooler months.

This is why heavy meals, excessive spice, alcohol, and irregular eating hit differently in summer. The system is redistributing resources, not getting weaker. It's managing the external heat load, which means less capacity available for the internal one.

What supports agni in summer is lighter food, adequate hydration, and eating at consistent times. Simple, easily digestible meals eaten before the heat of the day peaks. Not ice cold water, which douses the fire directly. Room temperature, or warm.

The system needs to work lesser in summer.

Leave a comment

How Stress Disrupts Agni

When the nervous system perceives stress - whether it's a difficult conversation, a looming deadline, or simply the low-grade hum of too many inputs across the day - it activates the sympathetic response. The body prepares for action. Blood moves to the muscles, the heart rate increases, cortisol rises.

And digestion shuts down. The gut is directly governed by the enteric nervous system - sometimes called the second brain - and it is exquisitely sensitive to stress signals. When the system is in fight-or-flight, digestion is not the priority - survival is.

The problem is that most people are running a low-grade stress response most of the time. Not necessarily acute danger, just chronic background pressure. And the gut, receiving the signal that this is not a safe time to digest, does exactly what it's told.

Agni dims > Digestion slows > Ama accumulates.

In Ayurveda, there is a specific term for agni disturbed by mental and emotional factors: vishama agni - irregular, variable fire. One day it works, the next it doesn't. Strong appetite one morning, none the next. This is the digestive pattern most commonly seen in people under chronic stress, and it is almost always accompanied by the kind of inconsistency we looked at in the earlier pieces on practice - the system trying to function without the stability it needs.

Modern Habits That Weaken Agni

Most of what modern life asks of the digestive system runs directly counter to what agni needs.

Eating at irregular times.

Agni, like all aspects of the body's intelligence, works best with rhythm. The digestive fire anticipates when food is coming - it prepares, it primes, it shows up. When meals are unpredictable, agni becomes unpredictable too.

Eating while distracted.

The parasympathetic nervous system - rest and digest - needs to be active for digestion to work properly. Eating while working, scrolling, or in the middle of a difficult conversation keeps the system in a mild stress state. The food arrives but the conditions for processing it do not.

Cold and raw food in excess.

Cold directly suppresses agni. Raw food requires more digestive fire to break down. Neither is harmful in moderation - but as dietary staples, particularly in an already stressed or depleted system, they tax the fire rather than support it.

Late night eating.

Agni follows a natural rhythm that mirrors the sun. It peaks around midday and quiets in the evening. A heavy meal at 9pm is asking the digestive fire to work at its lowest point. What doesn't get processed before sleep becomes ama.

Eating before the previous meal has digested.

Ayurveda recommends waiting until genuine hunger returns before eating again - not clock hunger, but actual appetite. Layering food on top of an incomplete digestive process is the equivalent of adding wood to a fire that hasn't finished burning the last load.

Share

Agni, Skin, and Mood - The Connections Most People Miss

The skin and the gut share the same embryonic origin - both develop from the ectoderm. In Ayurveda, this relationship is understood as a direct one: the skin reflects the state of digestion.

When ama accumulates in the gut, it eventually moves through the channels of the body - srotas - and surfaces wherever it can. For many people, that is the skin. Dullness, breakouts, uneven tone, inflammation - these are often less a skin problem than a digestion problem expressing itself outward.

This is also why topical solutions rarely resolve chronic skin issues completely. The root is internal.

The mood connection is equally direct, and increasingly supported by the research on the gut-brain axis. The gut produces the majority of the body's serotonin. When digestion is compromised, when ama is present, when the enteric nervous system is dysregulated - mood follows. Irritability without clear cause, low-grade flatness, difficulty feeling settled - these are frequently symptoms of agni that has been chronically under-supported.

The gut is not just related to mood, it is one of its primary sites.

Simple Ways to Support Agni Daily

These are not dramatic interventions. They are small adjustments that compound over time - the same logic as everything else in this Substack.

Eat your largest meal at midday

- when agni is naturally strongest. Even shifting lunch to be more substantial than dinner makes a noticeable difference over time.

Sit down to eat without a screen.

Five minutes of actually tasting food activates the parasympathetic response. Digestion begins in the mouth - the moment of attention is not incidental, it is part of the process.

Start the day with warm water.

Before anything else. It gently wakes the digestive fire without overwhelming it - only if this suits you.

Notice your appetite before eating.

Not the clock, not habit, not boredom-actual hunger. That signal is agni speaking. Learning to hear it is the beginning of eating in a way the system can actually use.

Give the gut a pause in the evening.

The last meal ideally three hours before sleep. Not as a rule, but as a gift to the system that will be doing its quieter work - repair, restoration, processing - through the night.

Visit the website to learn more

Agni as a Daily Practice

In Ayurveda, supporting agni is not a diet. It is a relationship with the body's intelligence - one that requires the same quality we have been exploring throughout this Substack.

Attention. Rhythm. Honest observation of what is actually happening rather than what habit or convenience dictates.

When agni is strong, the body transforms what it receives. Food becomes energy. Experience becomes wisdom. Even difficulty becomes something the system can digest and move through.

When it is weak, things accumulate. Not just in the gut - in the mind, in the mood, in the skin, in the subtle sense that something is not quite moving the way it should.

The fire doesn't need to be forced. It needs to be tended.

title: Ishvarapranidhana | Beyond Surrender
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
Why does the most discussed limb of Kriya Yoga remain the most misunderstood? And what happens to practice when surrender is replaced by something deeper — trust?

Ishvarapranidhana.

A word that gets translated, discussed, and debated more than almost any other term in the yogic framework. And yet the translation that travels most widely surrender to God, surrender to the divine misses the quality that makes it a living practice rather than a philosophical position.

What Ishvarapranidhana Actually Means

Patanjali introduces it in Sutra II.1 as the third limb of Kriya Yoga:

tapaḥ svādhyāya īśvarapraṇidhānāni kriyāyogaḥ

And returns to it in Sutra II.45:

samādhi siddhir īśvara praṇidhānāt

From ishvarapranidhana comes the perfection of samadhi.

The word breaks down precisely. Ishvara the supreme principle, the source. Prani toward, with intention. Dhana to place, to offer, to rest. A deliberate, conscious placing of oneself toward something larger, not a passive falling that surrender implies.

Surrender is not wrong. But it carries a connotation of defeat, of giving up what you wanted because you had no choice. Ishvarapranidhana is not that. It is the active, willing, and intelligent release of the grip that the practitioner maintains on outcomes, on progress, on the story of how things should unfold.

The closer translation is trust. And trust changes everything.

What We Have Lost in Modern Times

Trust, in the deepest sense, requires safety. The felt sense that the ground will hold. That what you release will be received. That the intelligence operating through and beyond you is not indifferent to your unfolding.

Modern life has systematically dismantled the conditions that make this felt sense available.

The nervous system under chronic stress doesn’t trust, it monitors and controls. It plans for every contingency because it has learned, through repeated experience, that relaxing vigilance has a cost. Let’s not call this weakness, it is the body’s intelligent response to an environment that rarely signals genuine safety.

But a nervous system in this state cannot practice ishvarapranidhana. Not really. It can think about surrender. It can understand it conceptually. But the actual release and the genuine placing of oneself toward something larger requires a nervous system that has been allowed to settle enough to believe that settling is safe.

This is why rhythm matters. Why agni matters. Why every earlier piece in this series has been, in some sense, preparing the ground for this one.

Share

Shraddha, The Bridge Between Trust and Faith

There is a word that sits at the heart of ishvarapranidhana and is rarely named alongside it.

Shraddha.

Usually translated as faith. But again, the translation is incomplete. Shr- the heart. Dha- to place, to hold. Shraddha is what you place in your heart and hold there. Not belief in the intellectual sense or he acceptance of propositions but the quality of orientation that arises when trust has been cultivated long enough to become stable.

Krishna speaks to shraddha directly in the Gita. In Chapter 17 verse 3, he says:

śraddhāmayo ‘yaṁ puruṣo

the person is made of their shraddha. What you hold in your heart with genuine trust is what you become. As within so without. The mere principle of manifesting your innerworl.

Shraddha is what makes ishvarapranidhana a practice rather than an event. You do not surrender once and remain surrendered. You return to trust, again and again, each time the nervous system has quietly contracted back into control. Each return is shraddha in action.

Flow | When Ishvarapranidhana Is Present

We explored sahaj in an earlier note - the quality of action that is no longer in conflict with how it is being done. And wu wei - the Taoist principle of movement that arises from the nature of things rather than from resistance to them.

Both are descriptions of what happens when ishvarapranidhana is genuinely present.

Flow, in the psychological sense Csikszentmihalyi described, and in the older sense the traditions have always known is not produced by effort. It arrives when the one who is efforting has temporarily stepped back. When the practitioner stops directing and starts listening. When trust is present enough that the intelligence of the moment can move through without being intercepted by the need to control it.

This is ishvarapranidhana made experiential. Not only by a philosophical stance but also a felt quality of practice and of life when the grip has genuinely loosened.

The reason flow states feel so extraordinary in modern life is precisely because genuine trust has become so rare. The nervous system, briefly released from its vigilance, remembers what it is like to move without resistance. That remembering is not a peak experience. It is a homecoming.

Visit Ascend's website

Ishvarapranidhana Is Not Passivity

This is the misreading worth naming directly.

Surrender and by extension, trust is frequently confused with inaction. With spiritual bypassing dressed in the language of acceptance. With the use of “I’m surrendering the outcome” as a reason not to show up fully.

Patanjali is precise on this. Ishvarapranidhana is the third limb of Kriya Yoga, the yoga of action. It sits alongside tapas and svadhyaya, alongside discipline and honest self-study. These three are not meant to be sequential and can also be simultaneous. The action is full. The self-study is honest. And the outcome is released.

This is nishkama karma from the Gita expressed as a living quality rather than a philosophical instruction. You act completely. You release completely. Not one after the other but together, as one movement.

The practitioner who waits for certainty before acting is not practicing ishvarapranidhana. They are practicing control under a different name.

The Thread That Was Always Here

Looking back across this series - rhythm, attention, dharana, sahaj, svadhyaya, the badhaka tattvas, viveka, santosha, tapas - ishvarapranidhana was present in each one.

It was there in the invitation to notice where your day feels scattered rather than forcing it into order. In the instruction to let dharana emerge rather than manufacture it. In the recognition that sahaj cannot be aimed at. In the tapas that burns without needing to control what the fire produces. In the santosha that does not require conditions to be right before allowing ease.

Every piece was, in some sense, a different angle on the same movement - the gradual, consistent loosening of the grip that prevents what is already present from being recognised.

Ishvarapranidhana is not the conclusion of practice. It is the quality that was always running beneath it.

Tapaḥ svādhyāya īśvarapraṇidhānāni. Three limbs. One fire. One honest look. One open hand.

A Practical Note on Cultivating Trust

Trust is not manufactured through technique. But conditions can be created in which it becomes more available.

Rhythm before surrender. A nervous system that has been given consistent anchors - regular meals, steady sleep, moments of genuine quiet - begins to signal safety to itself. Ishvarapranidhana becomes accessible when the body has stopped bracing.

Shraddha as daily orientation. Before practice and before the day begins, a moment of consciously placing yourself toward something larger. An acknowledgment that the intelligence moving through things is not yours to direct, only to align with.

Noticing flow when it arrives. Rather than trying to produce flow, practice recognising it when it appears, however briefly, however ordinarily. The conversation that moved without effort. The session where the body led and the mind followed. The moment of genuine ease. Each recognition strengthens shraddha. Each time you notice that trust produces something effort couldn’t, the nervous system learns that release is safe.

Brahmarpanaṁ - the offering of action. The Gita’s instruction to offer the fruits of action to something beyond the self. The work is done fully. The result is placed in the open hand of something larger. Over time this becomes less an instruction and more a natural quality of how action moves.

What Comes Next

The sadhaka tattva series has one more piece remaining.

Vairagya - non-attachment. The genuine freedom from dependency on outcomes, experiences, and the forms practice takes.

It is the direct counterpart to raga - the clinging we will look at on the badhaka side, and in many ways the quality that makes everything named in this series sustainable over time.

Where ishvarapranidhana asks you to open the hand, vairagya asks you to examine what you were holding so tightly - and why.

title: Tapas - The Heat That Purifies
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What is the difference between discipline that builds and discipline that burns? Between the effort that accumulates identity and the heat that dissolves it? Why does Patanjali name tapas not as a practice of self-improvement but as a means of thinning the kleshas themselves?

Simply put, this is Tapas/ tapa/ tapaha/ tapah. Fair warning, I’ve used them all

Tapa in Yoga

Beyond Discipline

Tapas is the first of the three limbs of Kriya Yoga. Most practitioners encounter it early as discipline, as austerity, as the commitment to show up even when it is inconvenient. And it includes all of that.

But tapas as sadhaka tattva and a supporting principle rather than simply a foundational one points at something more specific.

The word comes from the root tap - to heat, to burn, to generate warmth. In the Vedic tradition, tapas is the heat of the sun that causes seeds to germinate. The heat of the forge that transforms raw ore into something refined. Not the heat of destruction but the heat of transformation.

This distinction matters enormously in practice.

Tapas as discipline asks: did I show up?

Tapas as purifying heat asks: what was burned away by the showing up?

Subscribe now

Patanjali on Tapas

Sutra II.1 and II.2

Patanjali introduces tapas in Sutra II.1 as the first limb of Kriya Yoga:

tapaḥ svādhyāya īśvarapraṇidhānāni kriyāyogaḥ

Tapas, svadhyaya, ishvarapranidhana - the yoga of action. We have visited this sutra across several pieces in this series. But it is Sutra II.2 that reveals what tapas is actually for:

samādhibhāvanārthaḥ kleśatanūkaraṇārthaś ca

For the purpose of cultivating samadhi and for thinning the kleshas.

Two purposes. Both significant.

The first - cultivating samadhi, it’s what most practitioners focus on. Practice deepens, awareness expands, the movement toward stillness accelerates.

The second is less discussed and more immediately practical: klesha tanukarana, the thinning, the attenuation, the gradual weakening of the obstructing forces. Not their elimination in a single dramatic moment, but their progressive reduction through sustained heat.

This is tapas as purification. Not building something new, burning away what obscures what was always present.

What Tapa is Meant to Burn

Across this series we have looked at the badhaka tattvas - the obstructing principles. Rigidity, prayas, asmita, and the kleshas they express. What Patanjali is saying in II.2 is that tapas, rightly understood and rightly applied, is the heat that thins these obstructions directly.

By sustained warmth applied consistently over time and not by force or suppression.

Consider what heat does to a knot in a muscle. Forced stretching tears. But sustained warmth - gentle, consistent, patient - allows the tissue to release on its own terms. The knot doesn’t disappear in one session. But it thins. And over time, what was rigid becomes responsive.

This is klesha tanukarana made physical. And it maps precisely onto what happens in the subtler dimensions of practice.

The rigidity that prevents practice from evolving - tapas, applied with patience rather than force, gradually warms it until it can move again.

The prayas that drives practice compulsively - tapas as the commitment to show up even when the showing up is quiet, ordinary, unremarkable - slowly burns away the need for intensity.

The asmita that constructs a practitioner identity - tapas as the heat of sustained practice that eventually burns away what practice is not meant to serve.

Each klesha thins not through direct attack but through the consistent application of heat that simply does not stop.

Tapas vs performative Tapas

Performing tapas looks like: the cold plunge done for the identity of someone who does cold plunges. The fast undertaken to feel like a serious practitioner. The advanced asana practiced for the confirmation that effort has produced results. These generate heat, but it is the heat of the ego’s furnace, and what gets burned in that furnace is not the ego itself but the practitioner’s capacity for genuine surrender.

Purifying tapas looks quieter. It is the return to practice on the days when nothing dramatic is happening. The sitting that feels ordinary. The breath work done without expectation of result. The commitment sustained not because it is producing visible transformation but because the direction is clear and the heat is real whether or not it is felt in any given session.

Patanjali’s tapas is the second kind - The dirgha kala (long time) of Sutra I.14. The nairantarya uninterrupted continuity. Not intensity. Duration. Not spectacle. Sincerity.

Tapas and Agni, The Physical Dimension

In Ayurveda, which shares its metaphysical roots with the yogic tradition, agni- the transformative, sometimes digestive fire- is the physical expression of the same principle. What cannot be digested accumulates as ama - unprocessed residue that eventually becomes the root of disease.

This is also why the agni piece in this series belongs alongside the sadhaka tattvas thematically. A body with strong, balanced agni is a body in which tapas can do its work. When agni is weak, through irregular rhythm, poor sleep, chronic stress - the fire of practice cannot burn cleanly. The heat dissipates before it reaches what needs to be transformed.

Supporting agni is, in this sense, supporting tapas. They are the same fire at different levels of the system.

Tapas as the Heat That Reveals

There is a third dimension of tapas that sits between purification and discipline, and it may be the most honest description of what practice actually feels like from the inside.

Tapas reveals.

When you sit in the heat of sustained practice - not the peak session or the inspired day, but the ordinary Tuesday when the mind would rather be anywhere else - what arises is not always transformation. Sometimes it is simply what is there. The resistance. The restlessness. The pattern that has been running beneath awareness and now, with nowhere to go, becomes visible. (I have one such day documented and can share my experience soon.)

The kleshas do not thin by being avoided. They thin by being seen clearly, repeatedly, without the practitioner immediately trying to fix what is being revealed. This is where tapas and svadhyaya are most intimately connected. The heat creates the conditions. The honest self-study receives what the heat brings to the surface.

Together they form the intelligence at the centre of Kriya Yoga discipline that generates heat, self-study that reads what the heat reveals, surrender that releases the need to control what the heat produces.

Tapaḥ svādhyāya īśvarapraṇidhānāni. Three limbs. One movement.

A Practical Framework for Tapas as Purifying Heat

Consistency over intensity. The question is not how hot the fire burns in any single session but whether it is still burning tomorrow. A small, steady flame transforms more than an occasional bonfire followed by cold ash.

Ordinariness as practice. Asmita feeds on the extraordinary session. Tapas as purification happens most reliably in the unremarkable ones - the practice that asks nothing dramatic of the identity, and burns quietly regardless.

Noticing what arises without immediately resolving it. When the heat of practice brings something uncomfortable to the surface - restlessness, resistance, a pattern you’d rather not see - the tapasvi response is to remain with it. Not to analyse it immediately, not to fix it, not to use it as material for the practitioner’s self-story. Simply to stay in the heat a little longer.

Returning after interruption without self-punishment. The continuity Patanjali describes in I.14 is not about perfection. It is about the direction being maintained even when the heat goes out temporarily. The re-lighting of the fire, done without drama, is itself an act of tapas.

Tapas and Klesha Tanukarana - What Thinning Actually Feels Like

It rarely feels like transformation. It feels like the thing that used to activate you activating you slightly less. The pattern that used to run for three days running for two. The resistance that once felt immovable having, at some point you can’t quite identify, become slightly more porous.

This is klesha tanukarana. More Cumulative than dramatic.

And it is only visible in retrospect - which is precisely why the practitioner who needs each session to confirm progress will miss it entirely. The heat is working beneath the level at which the ego measures results.

This is also, quietly, where ishvarapranidhana re-enters. The surrender to a process whose results are not available on demand. The trust that the fire is doing what fire does, whether or not the practitioner can see the ash.

What Comes Next

The next sadhaka tattva is ishvarapranidhana - surrender as active practice rather than passive resignation. Having looked at viveka, santosha, and now tapas, the third limb of Kriya Yoga arrives not as a conclusion but as the quality that makes the other two sustainable.

title: Asmita, The Practitioner Who Got in the Way of the Practice
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What happens when the very identity built around spiritual practice becomes the thing that prevents it from deepening? What is asmita in yoga, and why is the spiritual ego the most difficult obstruction to see?

This is not a rare problem. It may be the most common one.

Thanks for reading Ascend's Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

In the yogic tradition, it has a precise name.

Asmita.

What Is Asmita in Yoga?

Patanjali defines asmita in Sutra II.6:

dṛg darśana śaktyor ekātmatevāsmitā

The identification of the power of seeing with the instrument of seeing. The confusion of the witness, pure awareness, with the mechanism through which it operates.

In plain terms: asmita is the ego. But not ego in the colloquial sense of arrogance or self-importance. It is something more fundamental - the deeply conditioned belief that you are the one who is practicing, rather than awareness itself moving through the form of practice.

Asmita is the second klesha in Patanjali’s sequence. Sutra II.3:

avidyā asmitā rāga dveṣa abhiniveśāḥ

It arises directly from avidya - the root ignorance, the failure to see clearly what we actually are. When we do not know ourselves as atman - as pure, unbounded awareness we construct an identity from what is available. And for a practitioner, what is available is practice itself.

Asmita and the Spiritual Ego

In an earlier piece, we looked at spiritual bypassing - the use of spiritual language and practice to avoid genuine self-examination. What that piece named as the ego learning the vocabulary of transcendence is, in precise yogic terms, asmita in operation.

How Asmita Operates in Practice

The practitioner who has been practicing for years begins to carry that practice as identity. I am someone who meditates. I am someone who does yoga. I am someone who has done the work. These are not false statements. But when they become the primary relationship to practice, when the practice is less about what it reveals and more about what it confirms, asmita is operating.

It shows up in recognisable ways.

The defensiveness when a teacher offers a correction that contradicts what you’ve been doing. The subtle hierarchy between practitioners, those who practice more seriously and those who don’t. The resistance to beginning again, to not knowing, to the beginner’s mind that practice actually requires. The disappointment when a session doesn’t feel the way an experienced practitioner thinks it should feel.

Underneath all of these is the same movement: the ego using practice as a mirror to confirm its own significance rather than as a window into what lies beyond it.

The Veil and What Lies Beneath - Asmita

The great Vedantic declarations, the mahavakyas, are not only philosophical positions to be adopted, they’re essentially direct pointers to what asmita obscures. Let’s break down a few of them.

Aham Brahmasmi - I Am Brahman

From the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Not the small self, not the practitioner identity assembled from years of effort and accumulation - but the ground of all being. That is what I refers to when seen clearly. Asmita is the mistaken identification with the instrument rather than the source. Aham Brahmasmi is not a belief to adopt. It is the recognition asmita prevents.

Tat Tvam Asi - Thou Art That

From the Chandogya Upanishad. The recognition that what you are seeking and what you are seeking it with are not separate. The awareness looking for liberation is itself the liberated awareness. Asmita is the confusion that makes this feel impossible - the insistence that the seeker and the sought are different, that the practitioner must travel somewhere they are not yet.

Another well known saying + Asmita

Shivoham - I Am Shiva

From the Nirvana Shatakam of Shankaracharya. Perhaps the most direct dismantling of asmita available in the tradition. Shankaracharya moves systematically through everything asmita might claim as identity - the mind, the intellect, the senses, the body, emotion, ego - and negates each one.

Shivoham. I am Shiva. Not when the practice is complete. Not when the ego has been sufficiently dissolved. Now. As this awareness, reading these words, recognizing something it already knew.

The practitioner is the veil. What lies beneath it was never covered.

Neti, neti. Not this, not this.

What remains when every constructed identity has been seen through is Shiva - pure, unbounded, self-luminous awareness. Not as a future state. As what is already the case.

Check out Website

Working With Asmita - The Practice of Neti Neti

The traditional response to asmita is inquiry.

Neti neti - not this, not this. The systematic seeing-through of every identity the ego has assembled. Not to arrive at nothing, but to arrive at what was always present beneath the accumulation.

Returning to the witness. In any moment of practice - particularly when the ego is activated, defensive, or comparing - notice who is noticing. The awareness that observes the ego’s activity is not itself the ego. That noticing, sustained even briefly, creates distance from the identification that is asmita’s substance.

Holding the mahavakyas as lived inquiry rather than affirmation. Aham Brahmasmi is not a statement to believe. It is a question to sit with. If awareness itself is what I am - then who is the one who needs practice to confirm something? That question, returned to honestly, begins to loosen asmita’s grip without requiring dramatic dissolution.

Allowing practice to be ordinary. Asmita feeds on significance. The extraordinary session, the peak experience, the confirmation that something important is happening. When practice is allowed to be unremarkable - when you sit without needing it to mean something about you - the practitioner identity has nothing to stand on. What remains is simply the practice, moving through awareness, leaving no residue of self-importance behind.

Some honest questions worth sitting with:

Does your sense of who you are depend, even partially, on being someone who practices? When practice feels flat or ordinary, is there disappointment - not at the quality of the session, but at what it implies about you? Do you find it easier to talk about practice than to simply be changed by it?

The Paradox at the Heart of Asmita

Here is what makes asmita the most subtle badhaka tattva in this series. Again, it’s important to note that I’m not going through any definitive list of sadhak and badhak tattvas mentioned in texts- these are just a few to start with.

You cannot practice your way out of it.. easily. Because the one who is practicing is itself the problem. Every effort to dissolve asmita through practice risks strengthening the practitioner identity that is doing the dissolving. This requires surrender and more, I will elaborate in another piece. For now here’s an example of how to overcome the paradox laid out in the Gita.

Krishna does not tell Arjuna to stop acting, stop practicing, stop engaging. He tells him to act without the actor being staked on the outcome. Nishkama karma - action without the contamination of personal agenda. Not no self, but a self that is no longer the measuring instrument of every experience.

The movement out of asmita tends to arrive not through more effort but through the kind of honest seeing that viveka makes possible.

Leave a comment

Frequently Asked Questions About Asmita

What is the difference between asmita and healthy self-awareness? Healthy self-awareness - svadhyaya - involves honest observation of patterns, reactions, and tendencies without identification. Asmita is the step beyond: where observation becomes identity, and where the observed self becomes something to protect and confirm rather than simply see.

Can asmita arise in someone new to practice? Yes - though it tends to be more visible in experienced practitioners because they have more practice-identity to protect. In beginners it often shows up as over-identification with a particular teacher, lineage, or style before genuine understanding has developed.

Is the goal to eliminate the ego entirely? The mahavakyas suggest something more precise than elimination. Tat Tvam Asi - thou art That is not a statement about the ego disappearing. It is a recognition that what you fundamentally are was never the ego to begin with. The goal is not destruction but correct identification.

How does asmita relate to spiritual bypassing? Spiritual bypassing using practice to avoid genuine self-examination is asmita in operation. The ego has learned to use the language of transcendence to maintain its position. Both point to the same root: avidya, the failure to see clearly what we actually are.

What is the most direct practice for working with asmita? The tradition consistently points to neti neti - the systematic inquiry into what you are not - combined with the mahavakyas as living questions rather than beliefs. More as honest orientation toward what practice is actually pointing at than techniques to master.

What Comes Next

The next badhaka tattva is raga - clinging, attachment.

title: Spiritual Bypassing Is an Oxymoron
description: How to stay away from it by being honest in your practice
author: Ashima Sood
contentHtml:
This is a short one, and one I felt was worth pausing the Sadhak and Badhak Tattva series for.

The term spiritual bypassing has become common in wellness circles. It describes the use of spiritual practice to avoid psychological wounds, difficult emotions, or the hard work of genuine self-examination.

The intention behind naming it was useful. The term itself is a problem.

Because bypassing - the avoidance of what is real, the retreat into elevated language, the performance of transcendence - is not spiritual. It is one of the most sophisticated expressions of ego the human system produces.

What bypassing involves

The need to appear evolved. The discomfort with being seen as ordinary. The subtle superiority of someone who has “done the work” over someone who hasn’t. The retreat into concepts of non-attachment when genuine intimacy is being asked for. The use of surrender as a reason not to act. The use of presence as a reason not to feel.

Every single one of these is ego. Not ego transcended - ego operating through the vocabulary of transcendence.

Visit Ashima's website for more

This is what makes it particularly difficult to see in oneself. The ego, when it learns the language of spiritual practice, becomes fluent in its own concealment. It can cite the Gita while avoiding accountability. It can speak of compassion while maintaining careful distance from anyone who might actually need something from it.

A truly spiritual orientation - one grounded in genuine practice rather than the performance of it - moves in exactly the opposite direction. It dissolves the need for the performance. It makes the practitioner more present, more accountable, more human - not less.

The ego shrinks. It does not dress up.

So if bypassing is ego, the question becomes: how do you recognise it in yourself?

It rarely arrives as avoidance. It arrives more as elevation. A subtle lift away from what is difficult - into concept, into practice, into the idea of the thing rather than the thing itself.

Some signs worth sitting with honestly:

Do you reach for practice when an emotion becomes uncomfortable - not to meet it, but to escape it? Does your spiritual understanding make you more patient with others, or does it give you a quiet reason to disengage? When someone challenges you, do you feel grounded - or do you feel the need to protect something?

These questions are to not answer quickly.

Share

How to keep bypassing at bay

When you notice the ego resurfacing through the vehicle of practice, the response is not more practice of the same kind. It is a return to the body - which the ego, given enough time in the conceptual realm, tends to quietly abandon.

Three entry points:

Grounding and presence.

The ego lives in narrative - past or future, defended or projected. The body lives only here. Physical grounding - feet on the floor, hands on the earth, weight felt - is not a technique. It is a reorientation toward what is pratyaksha - direct perception, the first and most immediate means of valid knowledge in the Indian philosophical tradition. Not mediated by memory, inference, or the stories the mind constructs about experience. Just what is actually, undeniably present.

The ego cannot survive pratyaksha for long. It needs interpretation to exist.

Dharana.

Not as a concentration exercise, but as an honest return to the present object - the breath, the flame, the sensation in the hands. When the mind has been living in the elevated story it tells about itself, dharana asks it to come back to something specific, immediate, and unadorned.

Pranayama.

The breath is the most direct available link between the voluntary and involuntary nervous system. It is also the most honest mirror the body offers - it reflects the actual state of the system, not the story about the state. Nadi shodhana in particular - alternate nostril breathing - works directly on the balance between the solar and lunar channels, and has a quieting effect on the part of the system that generates and defends identity.

These are not fixes but invitations back to what is real before the interpretation of it.

Leave a comment

For those who want to go deeper

- the Vigyan Bhairav Tantra is worth sitting with seriously.

112 meditation techniques, most of them a few lines long, all of them pointing at direct experience rather than conceptual understanding. The Vigyan Bhairav Tantra doesn’t offer a framework for thinking about consciousness. It offers a door into it.

The difference is significant - and it is precisely the difference that bypassing is designed to avoid.

If you find yourself drawn to the more elaborate, conceptual aspects of spiritual reading, and less drawn to the practices that ask something direct of the body and attention - that gap is worth noticing. It is usually where the bypassing lives.

Genuine practice does not make you more spiritual in the way the ego imagines it.

It makes you more honest. More present. More willing to be ordinary.

The ego, in the end, cannot survive that.

title: Santosha - The Practice of Enough
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What is the quality that allows a person to practice without constantly measuring their progress? To work without being consumed by outcomes? To be fully in their life without the low-grade sense that something is still missing?

The yogic tradition has a precise word for it.

Santosha.

Usually translated as contentment. But contentment, in English, carries a slightly passive flavour - the satisfaction of someone who has stopped wanting. Santosha is not that.

It is one of the most active practices in the entire framework.

What Is Santosha in Yoga?

Santosha is the second of Patanjali’s niyamas - the personal observances that form the inner architecture of practice. He introduces it in Sutra II.42:

santoṣāt anuttamaḥ sukhalābhaḥ

From santosha comes the highest happiness.

Not moderate happiness. Not adequate happiness. Anuttama - unsurpassed, beyond which nothing higher exists.

This is a striking claim for something so quietly named. Patanjali is not talking about the happiness that comes from achievement, or peak experience, or the resolution of difficulty. He is pointing at something that is available independent of circumstances - a quality of ease that is not contingent on things going well.

This is what makes santosha a practice rather than a state (such as equanimity). It does not arrive when conditions are right. It is cultivated in the middle of conditions as they actually are.

Santosha in the Bhagavad Gita - Action Without Craving the Fruit

The Gita approaches the same quality from a different angle.

In Chapter 12, Krishna describes the qualities of the devotee who is dear to him - and santosha appears explicitly among them.

Santushta satatam yogi - the yogi who is always content.

But this is not the contentment of someone who has withdrawn from life. In the same verses, Krishna describes someone who acts, engages, relates - fully present in the world, but not destabilised by its outcomes.

This is the Gita’s central teaching made personal: nishkama karma - action without craving the fruit - is not indifference to what happens. It is full engagement without the self being staked on the result.

Santosha is the inner quality that makes this possible. It is the ground from which action can arise cleanly, without the distortion of grasping or aversion. You do what the moment asks. You release what you cannot control. The doing and the releasing are not in conflict because the self is not measuring its worth against the outcome.

Subscribe now

What Santosha Counters - The Seeking Mind

To understand santosha as a practice, it helps to look at what it directly opposes.

The mind that is always looking for the next thing. The practitioner who cannot fully inhabit the session they are in because they are already measuring it against the session they want to have. The person who completes something meaningful and feels, almost immediately, the pull toward what comes next.

This is not ambition. It is trishna - a word that appears across both yogic and Buddhist traditions, usually translated as craving or thirst. The deep-seated belief that satisfaction lives slightly ahead of where you currently are. That the next level, the next experience, the next version of yourself, will be the one that finally settles things.

Trishna is one of the subtlest badhak tattvas* - and we will return to it in that series. But here it is worth naming as the exact quality santosha meets and dissolves.

Not by suppressing the desire. Not by pretending the seeking isn’t there. But by cultivating, through practice, a quality of presence that is genuinely sufficient to itself. That does not need the next thing in order to feel whole.

*It’s important to note here that I am not covering The 6 Sadhak or The 6 Badhak Tattvas that are academically taught in Hatha Yog. I do cover those in my discussions and sessions.

Visit Website

Santosha Is Not Complacency

This is the misreading most worth addressing directly.

Santosha is frequently confused with settling - the acceptance of things that should be changed, the absence of aspiration, the spiritual justification for staying stuck. This is not santosha. It is its shadow.

The distinction viveka makes here is essential. (And this is where the two sadhaka tattvas begin to work together.) Viveka - clear discernment - can distinguish between what is genuinely enough and what the ego is defending because change feels threatening. Between the santosha that arises from actual sufficiency and the pseudo-santosha that is really avoidance dressed in the language of acceptance.

Genuine santosha does not prevent growth. It creates the conditions in which growth is no longer compulsive. You move forward because the situation genuinely calls for it - not because standing still feels intolerable.

This is also how the Gita frames it. The devotee Krishna describes is not inactive. They are fully engaged. But their engagement arises from clarity and love rather than from the anxiety of someone who cannot rest until they have arrived somewhere.

Santosha is what makes sustained, intelligent action possible over time. Not the burst of effort driven by dissatisfaction - but the steady, renewable kind that doesn’t deplete.

Santosha in Practice - What It Actually Looks Like

In the body. A session of practice where you are not measuring yourself against yesterday, against the teacher, against the version of the pose you once held. Where the breath is the honest metric rather than the shape. Where what is present today - even if it is less than what was present last week - is met without resistance.

This is santosha in asana. Not lowering standards. Releasing the comparing mind long enough to actually practice.

In the mind. The thought that arises and is noted without immediately being acted on. The feeling of incompleteness that is allowed to be there without urgency. The moment between finishing something and reaching for the next thing - held, briefly, with nothing added.

In daily life. The meal that is tasted rather than consumed on the way to something else. The conversation that is actually finished before the next one begins. The evening that is allowed to be quiet without needing to be productive.

These are not dramatic. They are the texture of a life in which santosha is present - not as a peak state, but as a recurring quality of attention.

Cultivating Santosha - A Practical Framework

Santosha is not cultivated by trying to feel content. That effort tends to produce its opposite - an awareness of how discontent you actually are.

It develops through the same conditions that support every other sadhaka tattva in this series.

Rhythm. A day with natural anchors - consistent meals, a steady sleep schedule, moments of genuine pause - creates a nervous system that is not chronically in search of resolution. The seeking mind is partly a dysregulated nervous system looking for relief. Rhythm reduces the noise that feeds it.

Pratyaksha - returning to direct perception. Much of trishna lives in the conceptual realm - in comparison, projection, and the story of what is missing. Coming back to what is actually, directly present - the breath, the body, the immediate sensory experience - interrupts the seeking before it gathers momentum.

Svadhyaya applied to craving. Honest observation of the seeking pattern itself. Not to judge it - to understand it. When does the mind reach for the next thing? What is present just before it does? This observation, sustained, begins to reveal the mechanism. And what is seen clearly begins to lose its automaticity.

The Gita’s practice of offering. Brahmarpanaṁ - the offering of action to something larger than the self. When the fruits of effort are genuinely released - not suppressed, but offered - the self stops being the measuring instrument of every outcome. This is ishvarapranidhana made practical in daily life. And it is, quietly, one of the most direct routes to santosha available.

Santosha and Ananda - The Happiness That Doesn’t Depend

Patanjali’s claim in Sutra II.42 - that santosha brings the highest happiness - points at something the Vedantic tradition names directly.

Ananda - not pleasure, not satisfaction, but the quality of joy that is inherent to awareness itself. Not produced by conditions. Not dependent on outcomes. Present when the obscuring layers - of seeking, comparing, measuring - have been temporarily stilled.

Santosha is not the cause of ananda. It is more accurate to say that santosha removes what prevents ananda from being recognised. The contentment is not manufactured - it is what remains when the compulsive search for it has, at least for a moment, stopped.

This is what Patanjali means by anuttama sukha - the unsurpassed happiness. Not because something extraordinary has been achieved. Because the ordinary has finally been allowed to be enough.

What Comes Next

The next sadhaka tattva in this series is tapas - but not tapas as discipline in the conventional sense. As the heat that purifies rather than the effort that performs. The distinction is subtle and significant.

title: Viveka - The Practice of Discernment
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What is the one quality that, when present, makes every other aspect of practice more intelligent - and when absent, allows even the most dedicated practice to drift?

The answer the yogic tradition gives is consistent across texts, teachers, and lineages - Viveka.

Usually translated as discernment. But like most Sanskrit terms, the translation is a beginning, not an arrival just like how no scripture is the end all.

What Is Viveka in Yoga?

Viveka is the capacity to see clearly - to distinguish between what is real and what is constructed, what is essential and what is conditioned, what the moment is actually asking and what the mind is projecting onto it.

In Patanjali’s framework, viveka is not a personality trait or a cognitive skill. It is a quality of awareness that develops through practice - specifically through the sustained combination of abhyasa and vairagya that we explored in the last note on prayas.

aviplavā vivekakhyātir hānopāyaḥ (II.26)

Uninterrupted discernment is the path to the cessation of suffering. Patanjali is saying that the capacity to see clearly- sustained, unbroken, applied to every moment is the practice itself.

A Note From Vedanta - Shankaracharya’s Sadhana Chatushtaya

In verse 3 of the Aparoksha Anubhuti, Shankaracharya names four preliminary qualifications - sadhana chatushtaya, the fourfold means without which deeper enquiry cannot begin.

Viveka is the first.

The four are:

  • Viveka - discrimination between the real and the unreal

  • Vairagya - dispassion, the loosening of attachment to outcomes and experiences

  • Shat sampat - six inner disciplines, beginning with sama (quieting of the mind) and dama (steadying of the senses)

  • Mumukshuta - sincere longing for liberation

Shankaracharya places viveka at the beginning because without it, the remaining three cannot be correctly understood or applied. Vairagya without viveka becomes indifference. Sama without viveka becomes suppression. Mumukshuta without viveka becomes the longing for liberation that avoids the honest seeing liberation actually requires.

(A photo of my personal notes on this verse is below - the margins tend to hold more than the text.)

Viveka is not one tool among many. It is what keeps the entire path honest.

Viveka as Moment-to-Moment Awareness

This is where viveka is most often misunderstood.

It is frequently treated as a faculty you apply to big decisions - which teacher to follow, which practice to adopt, which direction to take. And it includes that. But viveka in its full expression is not reserved for significant moments.

It is the quality of awareness present in every moment. Whether to push or rest in this breath. Whether this thought is pratyaksha - direct perception of what is actually here or a story the mind is constructing from memory and habit. Whether what you are feeling right now is a genuine signal from the body or the residue of yesterday.

This is viveka applied continuously. Not as vigilance, which is an effort, but as a natural clarity that develops when the obstructions to seeing clearly have been reduced.

This is also why it opens the sadhaka tattva series. It is the quality that directly counters both rigidity and prayas - the two badhaka tattvas we have looked at so far. Rigidity is what happens when we stop seeing clearly what practice is actually producing. Prayas is what happens when we stop seeing clearly what the body and moment are actually asking. Viveka is the restoration of that seeing.

Visit Website

Viveka and Sat-Asat - Distinguishing the Real from the Constructed

The Vedantic framework offers a precise lens here through sat and asat - being and non-being, the real and the unreal.

Viveka, in this context, is the ongoing practice of asking: what here is sat - enduring, essential, actually present? And what is asat - constructed, projected, a product of conditioning rather than direct perception?

This less a philosophical exercise and more a practical one.

When you sit down to practice and immediately reach for a familiar sequence without checking what the body needs - that is asat operating as habit. When you feel resistance in practice and immediately label it as laziness rather than enquiring into what it actually is - that is asat operating as assumption.

Viveka is the moment of pause between stimulus and response. The brief space in which genuine seeing becomes possible. And like all spaces in practice, it can be cultivated.

A Framework for Returning to Truth Through Viveka

When clarity is lost - when the mind is moving in narrative rather than resting in direct experience - there is a sequence worth returning to. Not as a rigid protocol, but as an orientation.

A short framework on returning to clarity - for when perception is no longer steady.

Access the framework

Viveka in the Hatha Yoga Tradition

In the body, viveka shows up as the capacity to distinguish between productive discomfort and harmful strain. Between the edge that opens and the edge that injures. Between the resistance worth moving through and the signal asking to be respected.

This is sthira sukha made intelligent. Steadiness and ease are not positions you find and hold - they are a continuously recalibrated relationship that requires viveka to maintain. Every breath in practice is an opportunity to ask: is this still sthira? Is there still sukha present? If not - what has changed, and what is actually needed now?

A practice informed by viveka does not look the same every day. It cannot. Because what is present is not the same every day.

How Viveka Develops Over Time

Viveka is not switched on. It deepens gradually, through the sustained practice of the conditions that allow it.

Svadhyaya creates the habit of looking. Pranayama and kriya like nadi shodhana settles the nervous system enough for genuine perception to become possible. Dharana trains the mind to stay with what is present rather than moving immediately to what is familiar.

And tapas - the disciplined return to practice even when nothing dramatic is happening - builds the ground on which viveka eventually becomes continuous rather than occasional.

This is Kriya Yoga (Sutra II.1) as a living sequence: discipline creates the conditions, self-study applies the intelligence, surrender releases the distortion of personal agenda. What remains, over time, is clarity.

Vivekakhyāti. Sustained discernment. The path Patanjali names as the end of suffering not because suffering is suppressed, but because the confusion that generates it has been seen through.

Leave a comment

A Note on Viveka and the Badhaka Tattvas

Rigidity stops seeing what practice is producing. Prayas stops seeing what the moment is asking. Both are expressions of avidya, the root klesha, and the failure of clear seeing.

Viveka is not the opposite of these (opposites are human constructs). It is the restoration of the seeing they have obscured.

This is why it opens the sadhaka tattva series. Not as a technique to add, but as the quality whose presence makes every other practice more honest, more responsive, and more alive.
