title: Prayas - When Effort Becomes the Obstacle
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What happens when a dedicated practitioner never misses a session, never skips a rep, never allows rest - and still finds their practice stagnating?

The answer is rarely what they expect.

It is not that they need more discipline. It is not that the practice needs to be more advanced. It is that the effort itself has become the obstacle.

In the yogic tradition, this has a name: prayas as badhaka tattva - the obstructing principle of overzealous effort. Not the absence of trying, but the inability to stop.

Subscribe now

What Is Prayas in Yoga?

Prayas means effort, exertion, striving. In its right proportion, it is essential - without it, practice doesn’t begin. But when effort becomes compulsive, when it carries the weight of identity, when rest is experienced as failure - prayas shifts from foundation to obstruction.

The Hatha Yoga Pradipika is explicit on this. Among the conditions listed under yoga nasa - the destruction of practice - it names prayascha: overzealousness, excessive effort. The tradition places it alongside instability and bad association as things that actively prevent what practice is meant to build.

This is not a minor caution. The tradition is saying plainly: effort without intelligence is not tapas. It is its own kind of obstacle.

Share

Ha and Tha - When the Solar Principle Dominates

Hatha yoga is frequently misread as a tradition of intensity. The images that travel -advanced asana, extreme pranayama, ascetic discipline - suggest that more is always the direction.

But hatha itself tells a different story.

Ha - sun. Tha - moon. Effort and ease. The active and the receptive. These are not a hierarchy. They are a relationship. The solar principle without the lunar becomes heat without light - drive without discernment. A practice that generates force but cannot use it intelligently.

When prayas dominates, the lunar quality disappears entirely. What remains is a system running on its own momentum - generating effort because effort is what it knows, not because the moment is actually asking for it.

How Overzealous Effort Creates Stress in Practice

This is where stress enters - not the productive stress of genuine challenge, but chronic low-grade stress that comes from a nervous system that has never been given permission to arrive.

The body is present. The breath is moving. The sequence is being completed. But underneath, something is braced. Something is always preparing for what comes next rather than meeting what is here.

That bracing is prayas in the body. And over time, it accumulates.

The practitioner who is overzealous rarely identifies as someone avoiding rest. They identify as someone taking practice seriously. The ego, here, has found one of its more convincing disguises - commitment as cover for compulsion.

Leave a comment

Patanjali on Effort and Release - Abhyasa and Vairagya

In Sutra I.12, Patanjali names the two foundations of stable practice:

abhyāsa vairāgyābhyāṁ tan nirodhaḥ

Sustained effort (abhyasa) and non-attachment (vairagya). These are not sequential - first effort, then release. They are simultaneous. Practice only stabilises when effort is held alongside the willingness to release the fruits, the progress, the identity of the one who is practicing.

Prayas as badhaka is what happens when abhyasa is present without vairagya. Effort without release. Doing without the capacity to stop doing.

The system can only perform and not deepen under these conditions.

Sthira Sukha - Why Overzealous Effort Is Self-Defeating

Patanjali’s instruction in Sutra II.46 - sthira sukham āsanam - names steadiness and ease as qualities that arise together.

Not steadiness first, then ease. Both, simultaneously, as a single quality of practice.

This is impossible in a system that is chronically braced.

Steadiness requires a nervous system that has been allowed to settle. Ease requires a body that trusts it will not be pushed past what it can meet honestly. When effort is compulsive rather than intelligent, neither condition is available.

The practitioner working hardest toward depth may be the one most actively preventing it.

Recognising Prayas in Your Own Practice

What I notice in the people I work with is that this badhaka often arrives wrapped in a personal narrative, coming from deep conditioning along with vasanas and samkskaras:

I am someone who doesn’t give up. I am someone who shows up no matter what.

These are not false. But when they become the primary relationship to practice, they leave no room for the practice to ask something different.

Some honest questions worth sitting with:

Do you experience rest as part of practice, or as its absence? When the body signals that it needs something different today, do you meet that signal or override it? Is there any part of your practice that is genuinely receptive - not performing receptivity, but actually open to being changed by what arises?

If the answer to that last question is unclear, prayas may be present.

How to Work With Prayas - Returning Ha and Tha to Relationship

The entry point is not dramatic.

Before you begin, pause. Not as a technique. As a genuine question to the body - what is actually needed today?

Then, whatever the answer is - meet it without immediately overriding it.

This is the lunar principle re-entering. The receptive quality of tha returning to its relationship with effort. Not replacing effort, but softening the grip that makes effort compulsive rather than intelligent.

That pause, practiced consistently, is how ha and tha return to balance. It is also, quietly, the beginning of viveka - the discernment that can distinguish between resistance worth moving through and resistance the body is using to ask to be heard.

Share Ascend's Substack

Prayas, Avidya, and the Klesha Connection

Like rigidity, prayas at its root is an expression of avidya - the first and foundational klesha. The failure to see clearly what is actually present. In this case: the inability to see that the effort has become the thing being practiced, rather than a vehicle for what practice is meant to serve.

This is why svadhyaya - honest self-study - is the necessary companion to tapas in Kriya Yoga (Sutra II.1: tapaḥ svādhyāya īśvarapraṇidhānāni kriyāyogaḥ). Discipline without self-study doesn’t remain discipline. It becomes prayas. The heat of tapas, without the light of svadhyaya, drives rather than refines.

What Comes Next

The antidote to both rigidity and overzealous effort is the same: the capacity to see clearly what is actually present, without the distortion of habit or compulsion.

In the yogic tradition, this capacity has a name.

Viveka.

The first sadhaka tattva - and the subject of the next note in this series.

title: Rigidity
description: When Practice Becomes Its Own Obstacle
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
In the last note, we looked at svadhyaya - the practice of honest self-study that keeps discipline alive and surrender intelligent. We touched briefly on what happens when that layer is missing.

Practice continues. But something hardens.

This is the first badhaka tattva we’ll look at in this series. An obstructing principle - not something that stops practice from happening, but something that stops it from moving.

Rigidity.

In Hatha yoga, the word hatha itself carries a tension that is easy to miss.

Ha - sun. Tha - moon.
Solar and lunar.
Effort and ease.
The active and the receptive.

The tradition doesn’t ask you to choose between them. It is describing a dynamic - two forces that, when held in relationship, create something neither produces alone. The practice lives in that relationship. Not in the dominance of one over the other.

Rigidity is what happens when ha takes over completely.

Share

The solar principle - discipline, structure, will - is essential. Without it, practice doesn’t happen. But when it becomes the only operating principle, something is lost. The lunar quality - receptivity, adaptability, the willingness to be moved by what practice reveals - begins to disappear.

What remains looks like practice. It follows the form. It shows up regularly. But it has stopped listening.

Patanjali offers a quiet corrective in Sutra II.46:

sthira sukham āsanam.

The seat - and by extension, the practice - should be steady and at ease simultaneously. Not steady, then at ease. Not mostly steady with some ease. Both, together, as a single quality.

Sthira without sukha is rigidity. A practice that is stable but not soft. Disciplined but not responsive. It holds its shape, but it cannot yield - and a practice that cannot yield cannot deepen.

What’s worth sitting with here is that sthira and sukha are not opposites to be balanced. They are qualities that arise together when the practice is meeting the practitioner honestly. When one is absent, it is usually a sign that the other has been forced rather than found.

Mental rigidity in practice is subtler than physical stiffness, and in some ways more obstructing. It lives in the attachment to a fixed form - the same sequence, the same duration, the same entry point, repeated without inquiry.

This is not consistency. Consistency is returning to practice. Rigidity is returning to the same practice regardless of what the body, breath, or moment is actually asking.

The distinction matters because they feel similar from the outside - and even from the inside, until you look closely. Both involve showing up regularly. Both involve a degree of discipline. But one is responsive and one is not.

A rigid practice has quietly made a decision: that the form is more important than what the form is meant to serve.

Leave a comment

This is avidya - the first and root klesha - operating through the structure of practice itself. Not ignorance in the dramatic sense. The quieter kind. The assumption that because something worked before, it is still working now. The failure to see clearly what is actually present.

What I notice in the people I work with is that rigidity rarely announces itself. It arrives gradually, dressed as dedication. The practice that once created openness starts to feel like an obligation. The sequence that once felt alive becomes a checklist. There is a subtle contraction - not in the body necessarily, but in the relationship to practice itself.

And because the form is still intact, it can go unexamined for a long time.

This is precisely why svadhyaya - honest self-study - is placed alongside tapas in Kriya Yoga. Discipline without self-study doesn’t remain discipline for long. It becomes rigidity. The heat of tapas, without the light of svadhyaya, hardens rather than refines.

When reflecting on badhaka tattvas, the question you may ask yourself is not whether you are practicing.

It is whether your practice is still moving.

Not dramatically. Not always toward something new. But alive - responsive to what is actually present rather than committed only to what has always been done.

If there is a fixed form you return to - ask not whether it is working, but whether you are still meeting it honestly. Whether ha and tha are still in relationship, or whether one has quietly taken over.

That noticing, as always, is where things begin to shift.

title: Svadhyaya
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
Across these notes, something has been quietly present in the background.

When we looked at rhythm, the invitation was to notice where the day feels scattered. When we looked at dharana, the question was: when does attention stay without effort, and what is present in those moments? When we looked at sahaj and consistency, the thread kept returning to the same place - honest observation of what is actually happening, rather than what we assume should be happening.

That movement - turning toward oneself with genuine curiosity - has a name in the yogic tradition.

Svadhyaya.

Patanjali places it at the centre of Kriya Yoga in Sutra II.1:

tapaḥ svādhyāya īśvarapraṇidhānāni kriyāyogaḥ.

Discipline, self-study, surrender to a higher principle. Three limbs, but not a sequence. They are meant to function together - each one informing and deepening the others.

Svadhyaya is the middle one. And in some ways, the most intimate.

Etymology

The word itself offers something.

Sva - the self. Adhyaya - to study, but also to move toward, to enter into. So svadhyaya is not observation from a distance. It is a turning toward oneself that is also, in some sense, a moving closer.

This is not introspection in the psychological sense - the looping, evaluative kind that tends to generate more noise than clarity. Svadhyaya is quieter than that. It is the practice of watching without immediately interpreting. Noticing without immediately fixing.

You sit, and instead of asking am I doing this correctly, you ask what is actually here?

That shift - from evaluation to observation - is subtle. But it changes everything about what practice reveals.

Kinds of Svadhyay

In the tradition, svadhyaya has two faces that are inseparable.

The first is inner - the ongoing study of one’s own patterns, reactions, tendencies. The quality of attention across the day. What the breath does under pressure. Where the mind goes when it is left alone. This is svadhyaya as lived practice - not confined to the meditation seat, but present in every moment where you are willing to look honestly.

The second is outer - the study of scripture, of teachings, of the words of those who have moved through this territory before. Adhyayana in this sense is not reading for information. It is reading to be met. You bring yourself to the text, and the text reflects something back. What lands, what resists, what opens - this too is data. This too is svadhyaya.

Share

These two faces are not separate practices. They are one movement, turned in two directions simultaneously. The outer study illuminates the inner landscape. The inner observation makes the outer study personal rather than abstract.

Without the inner, scripture becomes philosophy. Without the outer, self-observation can become circular - the mind studying itself with the very instrument that needs examining.

Together, they create something more complete.

Abhyas and other facets sans Svadhyay

This is also where tapah and ishvarapranidhana find their coherence. Discipline without self-study tends to harden - effort continues, but it loses sensitivity. Surrender without self-study can drift into passivity - release without discernment. Svadhyaya is what keeps both alive and honest. It is the intelligence within the practice, the part that quietly asks: what is this actually doing? What is it revealing? Where is it taking me?

What I notice in the people I work with is that svadhyaya is often the missing layer. There is practice, and there is effort, and sometimes there is surrender. But the willingness to look honestly - at the patterns, at the resistance, at what practice is actually producing versus what it is assumed to be producing - this is often where the real work begins.

And without it, something else can quietly take root.

Practice continues, but it begins to move in circles. The effort becomes familiar in a way that stops being useful. A certain rigidity sets in - not dramatic, but felt. The system keeps going, but it has stopped listening to itself.

In the yogic framework, this has a name: badhaka tattva - the obstructing principle. The quality that arises when practice hardens into habit without the intelligence of self-study to keep it alive. That will be the subject of the next note.

For now, the question svadhyaya asks is simpler: is what I am doing still in contact with why I began?

Subscribe now

It doesn’t require formal study, though study helps. It doesn’t require a particular tradition, though tradition provides a map.

It requires only a genuine willingness to look.

If these notes have been useful, it may be worth asking what they’ve revealed - not as ideas, but as mirrors. Which ones landed easily, and which ones created a quiet resistance? Where did you find yourself nodding, and where did something tighten?

That noticing is svadhyaya already.

You don’t need to begin. You only need to recognise that you already have.

title: Why Practice Feels Inconsistent
description: What if inconsistency isn't failure, but information
author: Ashima Sood
contentHtml:
After the last few notes - on attention, dharana, and sahaj, a question tends to arise naturally.

If all of this is true, why does practice still feel inconsistent? Why does it work some days and fall apart on others?

Most people assume inconsistency is a discipline problem. The inner narrative becomes: I need to be more committed. I need to try harder. But that’s rarely the full picture.

What I’ve noticed, both personally and in the people I work with, is that inconsistency usually comes from something more basic. The conditions for practice are not stable.

Subscribe now

You may sit down to practice, but the body is restless. Or the breath is uneven. Or the mind has been moving continuously since morning without a single real pause. In that state, practice becomes effortful. And effort, repeated without support, eventually drops.

This is where the earlier ideas connect directly.

Dharana is not something you force.

Sahaj - and this is worth saying carefully - is something you can orient toward. In some meditation traditions it is held as a sankalpa, a conscious intention seeded at the start of practice. Not a demand, but a direction. The difference matters. You are not grasping at effortlessness. You are simply making it the quality you are moving toward, and allowing practice to reveal it gradually.

As a sankalpa, sahaj functions differently than a goal. A goal is something you either reach or fail to reach. A sankalpa is something you return to - a remembering rather than an achieving. Over time, what began as an intention becomes recognisable as an emergent quality. You start to notice it arriving - briefly, unexpectedly - before you’ve done anything to produce it. That noticing is itself part of the deepening.

Leave a comment

What both dharana and sahaj depend on, though, is the capacity of the system to settle. And here is where abhyas - consistent, devoted practice - becomes the real subject.

Patanjali is clear on this. Practice becomes firmly grounded through long, uninterrupted, sincere engagement.

Sa tu dirgha kala nairantarya satkara asevitah dridhabhumih - I.14.

He says nothing about the conditions needing to be perfect. Abhyas is not contingent on having the right environment, the right time of day, the right state of body and mind. It is the practice itself, returned to with sincerity, that creates the ground.

So the question of inconsistency is not really about whether the conditions are right. It is about what you are bringing to practice when you show up - regardless of conditions.

That said, there is a practical intelligence in noticing what makes showing up harder than it needs to be. Not as a precondition for practice, but as svadhyaya - self-observation applied to your own patterns. If you are consistently sitting at a time of day when the body is exhausted, or attempting formal practice in the middle of continuous stimulation, it is worth asking whether that is devotion or unconscious resistance dressed as discipline.

The tradition doesn’t prescribe. But it does invite honesty.

So instead of asking why am I inconsistent, it can be more useful to ask: what am I actually bringing to practice when I arrive?

Is there sincerity? Is there a willingness to stay, even when it feels unremarkable? Is there a sankalpa - however quietly held - that orients the sitting toward something?

These questions tend to be more useful than restructuring the external conditions, though both have their place.

Over time, something shifts.

Practice becomes less of a negotiation. More of a return. Not because you’ve forced consistency, but because the practice itself has begun to create the ground it needs.

Abhyas and sahaj are not opposites - devoted effort and natural ease are not in conflict. One, sustained over time, becomes the other.

This is also where ishvarapranidhana re-enters. The willingness to practice without demanding a particular result - to show up sincerely and release the rest - is not separate from consistency. It is what makes consistency sustainable.

If your own practice has been uneven, you don’t need to fix everything at once.

Just look honestly at what you’re bringing when you arrive. And begin there.

title: What Effortlessness actually means
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
What Effortlessness Actually Means

In the last note, we looked at dharana - the capacity of the mind to remain with something without being held there by force.

There’s a related word that appears across yogic and devotional traditions, and it’s often misunderstood in a similar way.

Sahaj.

Usually translated as natural, effortless, innate.
But none of those quite capture it.

Sahaj isn’t ease in the casual sense.
It doesn’t mean doing nothing, or that practice should feel comfortable from the start.

It points to something more specific:

A state where what you are doing is no longer in conflict with how you are doing it.

Share

Most of us have felt this, even outside of practice.

A conversation that didn’t require effort.
Work that came together without strain.
A walk where the mind quieted on its own.

In those moments, you weren’t trying to be present.
You just were.

That’s closer to sahaj.

Not as something achieved,
but as something the system already knows.

The question is what interferes with it.

Subscribe now

The Taoist tradition speaks about something similar: wu wei.

It’s often translated as non-doing, but that’s misleading.

It’s not inaction.
It’s action that doesn’t force.

Water is the usual example.
It doesn’t push against the rock.
It finds its way around.

And over time, that is what shapes everything.

Leave a comment

What connects sahaj and wu wei - what sits quietly underneath both - is something Patanjali names in Kriya Yoga:

Ishvarapranidhana.

Usually translated as surrender.
But again, that word tends to be misunderstood.

It’s not passivity.
It’s not giving up.

It’s the recognition that you are not the only force at work.

There is an intelligence in the body,
in the breath,
in the unfolding of practice itself.

And when effort ignores that,
it tends to create friction rather than resolve it.

Wu wei asks:
Can you move with what is happening, instead of against it?

Ishvarapranidhana asks:
Can you act fully, and loosen your grip on the outcome?

Neither is about doing less.

Both are about listening more carefully.

Thanks for reading Ascend's Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

What gets in the way of flow is rarely laziness.

It’s effort applied in the wrong direction.

Pushing when something needs to settle.
Acting from agitation instead of clarity.
Holding too tightly to how something should unfold.

That grip shows up everywhere.

And it creates resistance at every stage.

Share Ascend's Substack

Ishvarapranidhana is the loosening of that grip.

Not abandoning effort,
but changing how it is held.

And when that happens - even slightly -
sahaj begins to appear on its own.

In the beginning, practice doesn’t feel like this.

There’s effort to sit.
Effort to stay.
Effort to return when the mind has already left.

There’s restlessness, impatience, negotiation.

That’s not a problem.
It’s just unfamiliar territory.

But if practice is met with steadiness, not force, something shifts.

The same actions - sitting, breathing, observing -
begin to require less.

Not because they’ve become automatic,
but because the friction has reduced.

You stop arguing with yourself about whether to begin.
The mind stops looking for an exit immediately.

This is where sahaj starts to show up.

Quietly.

Nothing dramatic.
But something has changed.

Many people try to reach this directly.

Effortlessness without going through effort.

But sahaj doesn’t work that way.

It’s not something you aim for.
It’s what remains when unnecessary effort drops away.

This is why rhythm, attention, and observation matter.

Without them, ease becomes avoidance.

With them, it becomes alignment.

Between intention and action.
Between effort and what is already present underneath it.

That last part is ishvarapranidhana in practice.

Not a belief.

A relationship with what you don’t fully control -
held with sincerity, not resistance.

What I notice in the people I work with is that this shift doesn’t announce itself.

There’s no clear before and after.

They just stop pushing quite as hard.

They begin to notice what the practice is actually asking,
instead of what they assumed it required.

The effort doesn’t disappear.

It becomes appropriate.

If you’re somewhere in the middle of your own practice,
unsure how much effort is right -

the question isn’t
how do I make this effortless?

It’s quieter than that:

Where am I adding effort that isn’t needed?
And what am I not willing to release?

Sahaj isn’t something you create.
Wu wei isn’t something you perform.
Ishvarapranidhana isn’t something you perfect.

They’re pointing to the same movement -

inward,
and toward a kind of trust
that effort alone can’t produce.

title: On Dharana: What It Means to Stay
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
In the last note, we touched on attention.

There is a word in the yogic framework that is often translated simply as “concentration.” But that translation misses something essential.

The word is dharana. (from the root dhri - to hold, to support. Not to grip.)

Dharana is the capacity of the mind to remain with something without immediately moving away.

This distinction makes all the difference.

Most people approach attention through force. They try to hold the mind in place. What they encounter instead is resistance - distraction, fatigue, a subtle irritation that makes the effort feel counterproductive.

This happens because the mind, in that moment, is not able to stay. And holding harder does not change that.

Dharana is not created by effort. It emerges when the conditions that allow the mind to remain are present.

If you observe carefully, you’ll notice there are moments when attention rests naturally - when you’re absorbed in something, when the body is at ease, when there is no internal urgency pressing from behind. In those moments, you are not trying to concentrate. You are simply not being pulled away.

That is closer to dharana.

What prevents it is not a lack of discipline. It is fragmentation of the mind.

The day is broken into too many small movements - constant stimulation, unfinished actions, irregular rhythm. The mind learns to move quickly, and repeatedly. Over time, stillness begins to feel unfamiliar.

So the work is not to “improve concentration” directly. It is to reduce what interrupts it.

When the body is allowed to settle, when the breath becomes less strained, when the number of competing inputs is reduced - the mind begins to stay. Not perfectly. But more often than before.

This is also why, in the classical sequence, dharana precedes both dhyana and samadhi. (Patanjali introduces these together as the inner limbs - dharana, dhyana, samadhi - in Sutras III.1 through III.3, collectively called samyama.)

Without the capacity to remain, even briefly, meditation becomes an effort to return - again and again, without resolution.

With dharana, something shifts. The returning reduces. The staying increases. What begins to open is not concentration in the effortful sense, but a kind of natural settledness.

What I’ve noticed in working with people is that this stage is rarely recognised.

There is an attempt to meditate, without first restoring the capacity to remain. So the experience becomes frustrating - not because the person is doing it wrong, but because a prior condition hasn’t been met.

When the conditions are adjusted - even slightly - the mind begins to show its natural tendency toward steadiness. It was always there. It simply needed the space.

You don’t need to force this.

Begin instead with observation:

When does my attention stay without effort? What is present in those moments?

That question, returned to with some regularity, begins to reorganise things quietly.

Dharana is not something you impose.

It is something you allow.

title: What Attention Is Actually Asking
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
After the last note, I’ve been thinking about attention.

Not concentration in the effortful sense - the kind where you sit down, clench, and try to focus.
But the quieter kind. The capacity to stay with something long enough for it to matter.

Most people I speak with aren’t struggling because they lack discipline.
They’re struggling because their attention has been pulled in so many directions, for so long, that returning to one thing feels almost uncomfortable.

This is worth pausing on.

In the Yoga Sutras, Patanjali offers a deceptively simple instruction:

Tapah svadhyaya ishvarapranidhana.

Discipline. Self-study. Surrender to something larger than the self.

Together, these form Kriya Yoga - not action as productivity, but action as a path toward clarity.

The one that tends to receive the least attention is the middle one.

Svadhyaya.

It is often translated as the study of sacred texts. And it includes that.
But at its root, it points to something more immediate:

The practice of turning observation (-dhyay) inward (sva-).

Of watching your patterns, your reactions, the quality of your attention -
with the same interest you might bring to anything else you are trying to understand.

This is where rhythm and attention meet.

When the day has no steadiness, when attention fragments across too many things, most people look outward for the fix -
a new system, a better routine, something to impose order from the outside.

Svadhyaya suggests a different starting point.

Before the fix - the noticing.

What actually happens to your attention across the day?
Where does it hold naturally?
Where does it leave before you’ve decided to let it go?
When do you feel most present, and when do you feel most scattered?

These are not abstract questions.
They are the beginning of practice.

In the yogic framework, the mind has a natural capacity called dharana - the ability to rest on something without immediately moving away. It quite literally refers to ‘flow’.

It doesn’t require force.
It returns when the conditions allow it,
and when you begin to understand what depletes it - in you specifically.

That understanding is svadhyaya.

Not a personality test.
Not journaling as performance.
Just honest, repeated observation of what is actually happening -
in the body, the breath, the quality of your days.

I’ve noticed in the people I work with that this step is often skipped.
There’s a clear sense that something needs to change,
but a much hazier sense of what is actually occurring.

So the practice, before any technique, is simply to look.

Start there.

Not with a solution.
With a question you’re willing to sit with:

When during my day am I actually present - and when have I already left?

Returned to with some regularity, that question begins to change things.

Not because insight alone transforms -
but because the act of watching yourself without judgment is itself a form of steadiness.

And steadiness, as we’ve been exploring, is where everything else begins.

title: Where this work begins
description: There is a point where information stops helping.
author: Ascend with Ashima
contentHtml:
There is a point where information stops helping.

You read more, listen more, try more - and yet something feels unchanged.
Not because you don’t understand, but because the pace at which you are living doesn’t allow anything to settle.

This is where practice (abhyasa) begins.

Not as intensity, but as a return to rhythm.

In the yogic traditions, clarity is not created by adding more.
It comes from removing excess movement - externally and internally - so that what is already present can be seen more clearly.

For many people today, the challenge is not lack of knowledge.
It is a constant state of low-level agitation - of the body, the breath, the mind.

Over time, this shows up as:

  • difficulty sleeping

  • scattered attention

  • emotional reactivity

  • a sense of being slightly out of sync

What begins to shift things is often very simple:

  • eating at consistent times

  • allowing the breath to slow down

  • moving the body without strain

  • sitting quietly, even for a few minutes

Not dramatic, steady.

This is the space I try to hold in my work - whether through yoga, Ayurveda, or scripture.

A space where things are not rushed, and understanding is allowed to deepen at its own pace.

If you’ve been feeling the need to slow down - not as an escape, but as a way to live more clearly - this is a good place to begin.
